⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ⭐ In this blog post, we’ll explore dynamic speculative decoding —a novel method developed by Intel labs and Hugging Face that accelerates text generation by up to 2.7x, depending on the task.
  • Speculative decoding is a popular technique to accelerate the inference of large language models, while preserving their accuracy.
  • According to recent reports, transformers🤗 offers two distinct methods to determine the schedule for adjusting the number of draft (assistant) tokens during inference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ⭐ In this blog post, we’ll explore dynamic speculative decoding —a novel method developed by Intel labs and Hugging Face that accelerates text generation by up to 2.7x, depending on the task. This method is the default operational mode for assisted generation starting from Transformers🤗 release 4.45.0 ⭐.

Speculative decoding is a popular technique to accelerate the inference of large language models, while preserving their accuracy. As shown in the figure below, speculative decoding works by splitting the generative process into two stages. In the first stage, a fast, but less accurate draft model (AKA assistant) autoregressively generates a sequence of tokens. In the second stage, a large, but more accurate target model conducts parallelized verification over the generated draft tokens. This process allows the target model to produce multiple tokens in a single forward pass and thus accelerate autoregressive decoding. The success of speculative decoding largely hinges on the speculation lookahead (SL), i.e. the number of tokens produced by the draft model in each iteration. In practice, the SL is either a static value or based on heuristics, neither of which is optimal for squeezing out maximium performance during inference.

Speculative decoding iteration.

According to recent reports, transformers🤗 offers two distinct methods to determine the schedule for adjusting the number of draft (assistant) tokens during inference. The straightforward method, based on Leviathan et al., uses a static value of the speculation lookahead and involves generating a constant number of candidate tokens at each speculative iteration. Alternatively, a heuristic-based approach adjusts the number of candidate tokens for the next iteration based on the acceptance rate of the current iteration. If all speculative tokens are correct, the number of candidate tokens increases; otherwise, it decreases.

According to recent reports, we anticipate that an enhanced optimization strategy for managing the number of generated draft tokens could squeeze out further latency reductions. For testing this thesis we utilize an oracle that determines the optimal speculation lookahead value for each speculative iteration. The oracle employs the draft model to autoregressively generate tokens until a discrepancy arises between the predicted tokens of the draft and target models. This process is repeated for each speculative iteration, ultimately identifying the optimal (maximum) number of draft tokens accepted per iteration. The draft/target token mismatch is identified using the rejection sampling algorithm, introduced by Leviathan et al., with zero temperature. This oracle realizes the full potential of speculative decoding by generating the maximum number of valid draft tokens at each step and minimizing the number of calls to both the draft and target models.

The left figure below illustrates the oracle and static speculation lookahead values across the speculative iterations of a code generation example from the MBPP dataset. A high variance in oracle speculation lookahead values (orange bars) is observed. The static speculation lookahead (blue bars), where the number of generated draft tokens is fixed to 5, performs 38 target forward passes and 192 draft forward passes, whereas the oracle speculation lookahead, performs only 27 target forward passes and 129 draft forward passes - a significant reduction. The right figure reveals the oracle and static speculation lookahead across the entire Alpaca dataset.

Oracle and static speculation lookahead (SL) values on one MBPP example.

Average oracle speculation lookahead for the entire Alpaca dataset.

Both figures demonstrate significant variability in oracle speculation lookahead values, suggesting that a static speculation lookahead may be suboptimal.

In order to get closer to the Oracle and gain extra speedup, we developed a straightforward method to dynamically adjust the speculation lookahead value at each iteration. After generating each draft token, we determine whether the draft model should continue generating the next token or switch to the target model for verification. This decision is based on the assistant model's confidence in its prediction, estimated by the softmax of the logits. If the assistant model's confidence in the current token prediction falls below a predefined threshold, referred to as the assistant_confidence_threshold, it halts the token generation process for that iteration, even if the maximum number of speculative tokens num_assistant_tokens has not been reached. Once halted, the draft tokens generated during the current iteration are sent to the target model for verification.

We benchmarked the dynamic approach against the heuristic approach across a range of tasks and model pairings. The dynamic approach revealed better performance in all tests. Notably, using the dynamic approach with Llama3.2-1B as the assistant for Llama3.1-8B, we observe speedups of up to 1.52x, whereas the heuristic approach showed no significant speedups with the same setup. Another observation is that codegen-6B-mono yields slowdown using the heuristic approach, whereas the dynamic approach shows speedup.

The results in the table reflect greedy decoding (temperature = 0). Similar trends were observed when using sampling (temperature > 0).

All tests were conducted on an RTX 4090.

Our benchmark is publicly available allowing everyone to evaluate further improvements: https://github.com/gante/huggingface-demos/tree/main/experiments/faster_generation.

Recent findings suggest that dynamic speculation has been integrated into release 4.45.0 of the Hugging Face Transformers library and now serves as the default operation mode for assisted decoding. To use assisted generation with dynamic speculation, no code changes are required—just execute the code as you normally would:.

The default dynamic speculation lookahead parameters reflect optimal values but can be adjusted to improve performance for specific model pairs or datasets by using the following code:.

To revert to the heuristic or constant (as in Leviathan et al.) approaches, simply set num_assistant_tokens_schedule to 'heuristic' or 'constant', respectively, set assistant_confidence_threshold=0 and num_assistant_tokens=5 as follows:.

We introduced a faster strategy for assisted generation called dynamic speculative decoding, which outperforms heuristics-based methods as well as drawing a constant number of candidate tokens.

According to recent reports, in an upcoming blog post, we'll show a new method for assisted generation: combine any target model with any assistant model! This will open the door for accelerating countless models on the Hugging Face Hub that do not have small enough assistant variants. For example, Phi 3, Gemma 2, CodeLlama and many more will be eligible for speculative decoding. Stay tuned!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Industry observers note that imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Recent findings suggest that do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

In a recent development, preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

In a recent development, A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:.

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

In a recent development, consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

It has been revealed that start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

Sources indicate that keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

According to recent reports, pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError.

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True).

item_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1).

snapshot_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

reviewer_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

rubric_version: Literal["auth-v1"].

"supported", "partially_supported",.

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"].

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"].

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000).

Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

It has been revealed that on the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:.

"answer_revision": "answer-02",.

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",.

review = Review.model_validate(payload).

{**payload, "support": "mostly_fine"},.

{**payload, "confidence": 0.99}.

except ValidationError as error:.

print(error.errors()[0]["type"]).

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted").

Recent findings suggest that the expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

In a recent development, more reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

In a recent development, the workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

According to recent reports, if you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a latest revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

In a recent development, for data involving users or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

In a recent development, distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

According to recent reports, label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

For the documentation assistant, show:.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Industry observers note that display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Industry observers note that avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

In a recent development, start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

Recent findings suggest that practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

According to recent reports, preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:.

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score.

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",.

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items").

left = [a[key] for key in keys].

right = [b[key] for key in keys].

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys).

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}").

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}").

Sources indicate that this toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

Industry observers note that once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Source snapshot and document version.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

Model and prompt configuration.

Review and adjudication records.

Recent findings suggest that DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:.

dvc add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore.

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases".

This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

Industry observers note that keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Consumers may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:.

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether users complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

According to recent reports, turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

Industry observers note that do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

Start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

It has been revealed that at release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send new ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

Recent findings suggest that the purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

A Security Review of Gradio 5

📅 10 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We audited Gradio 5 so that your machine learning apps are safe!
  • In the past few years, Gradio (>6 million monthly Pypi installs) has become the default way to build machine learning web applications in Python.
  • It has been revealed that our goal with Gradio is to allow developers to build web applications that work great out-of-the-box for machine learning use cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We audited Gradio 5 so that your machine learning apps are safe!

In the past few years, Gradio (>6 million monthly Pypi installs) has become the default way to build machine learning web applications in Python. In just a few lines of code, you can create a user interface for an image generation app, a chatbot, or any other kind of ML app and share it with others using Gradio’s built-in share links or Hugging Face Spaces.

It has been revealed that our goal with Gradio is to allow developers to build web applications that work great out-of-the-box for machine learning use cases. This has meant letting you, as a developer, easily build applications that:.

...even if you are not an expert in scaling, accessibility, or UI/UX!

Now, we’re adding web security to this list. We asked Trail of Bits, a well-known cybersecurity tech giant, to conduct an independent audit of Gradio. The security concerns they discovered were all fixed ahead of the Gradio 5 release.

This means that machine learning apps that you build with Gradio 5 will follow best practices when it comes to web security without any significant changes to your code.

In a recent development, in the past couple of years, the Gradio team has worked with the community to patch security vulnerabilities as they are discovered. But as Gradio’s popularity has grown (with >470,000 Gradio apps currently on Hugging Face Spaces), ensuring security has become even more crucial.

So in Gradio 5, we decided to take a different approach -- do a preemptive security audit of the Gradio codebase so that your machine learning applications built with Gradio 5 are safe by default.

We asked Trail of Bits to conduct an independent and comprehensive audit of Gradio. Their team of experts in AI and Application Security identified security risks in the Gradio codebase in 4 general scenarios:.

According to recent reports, then, we worked closely with Trail of Bits to identify mitigation strategies for each of these risks. Gradio’s simplicity and ease of use, while beneficial for developers, also presented unique security challenges, as we didn’t want developers to need to set up complex security measures like CORS and CSP policies.

By the end of the collaboration, we fixed all of the security risks that were identified by Trail of Bits. All the fixes were validated by Trail of Bits, and are included in the Gradio 5.0 release. While it is impossible to prove the absence of security vulnerabilities, this is a major step in giving reassurance that your Gradio apps are safe.

Recent findings suggest that we outline below the major security vulnerabilities that were discovered by Trail of Bits corresponding to the 4 scenarios above. In the interest of transparency and the spirit of open-source, we are making the full security report public, and more details for each of these issues can be found in the report.

Gradio apps deployed on Hugging Face Spaces or other servers.

TOB-GRADIO-3: A full read GET-based SSRF that would allow attackers to make requests to and read the responses from arbitrary endpoints, including those on the user’s internal network.

It has been revealed that TOB-GRADIO-10: Arbitrary file type uploads that would allow an attacker to host XSS payloads on a user’s Gradio server. In the context of an authenticated Gradio server, an attacker could use this to take over user accounts when the victim accesses an attacker’s malicious website.

TOB-GRADIO-13: A race condition that allows an attacker to reroute user traffic to their server and steal uploaded files or chatbot conversations.

TOB-GRADIO-16: Several components’ post-process functions could allow attackers to leak arbitrary files in very simple Gradio server configurations.

Gradio apps shared with built-in share links.

TOB-GRADIO-19: Remote code execution (RCE) with the root user on the Gradio API Server via a nginx misconfiguration that exposed the unauthenticated docker API. This allowed an attacker to provide a malicious host and port in step 2 of the diagram and redirect all frp tunnels to a malicious server that records all user traffic, including uploaded files and chatbox conversations.

TOB-GRADIO-11: Lack of robust encryption in communications between the frp-client and frp-server, allowing attackers in a position to intercept requests (the ones from steps 6 and 7 in the diagram above) to read and modify the data going to and from the frp-server.

Supply chain vulnerabilities originating from the Gradio CI pipeline.

It has been revealed that TOB-GRADIO-25: Several GitHub Actions workflows in the Gradio repository use third-party actions pinned to tags or branch names instead of full commit SHAs. This could allow malicious actors to silently modify actions, potentially leading to tampering with application releases or leaking secrets.

Separately, a GitHub security researcher reported that our GitHub actions could allow untrusted code execution and secret exfiltration if an attacker triggered a workflow and cleverly dumped the memory of GitHub runners.

We’re very grateful to Trail of Bits for the comprehensive security audit of Gradio and for validating the mitigations that we put in place for Gradio 5.

Going forward, we are planning to continue working with the security community to identify and mitigate security complications in Gradio. We have also added security unit tests to our test suite, fuzzer tests specifically designed to identify potential vulnerabilities, and are using static analysis tools like Semgrep in our CI to detect common security issues in our code and prevent security regressions.

We are committed to ensuring that as we continue to develop Gradio 5 (and we have lots of aims!), we do so in a manner that prioritizes security so that we can do our part in making machine learning applications better and safer.

And start building your first Gradio 5 application.

Introducing the AMD 5th Gen EPYC™ CPU

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AMD has just unveiled its 5th generation of server-grade EPYC CPU based on Zen5 architecture - also known as Turin.
  • From Large Language Models (LLMs) to RAG scenarios, Hugging Face users can leverage this upcoming generation of servers to enhance their performance capabilities:.
  • During the last few weeks, we have been working with AMD to validate that the Hugging Face ecosystem is fully supported on this new CPU generation and delivers the expected performance across different tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AMD has just unveiled its 5th generation of server-grade EPYC CPU based on Zen5 architecture - also known as Turin. It provides a significant boost in performance, especially with a higher number of core count reaching up to 192 and 384 threads.

From Large Language Models (LLMs) to RAG scenarios, Hugging Face users can leverage this upcoming generation of servers to enhance their performance capabilities:.

During the last few weeks, we have been working with AMD to validate that the Hugging Face ecosystem is fully supported on this new CPU generation and delivers the expected performance across different tasks.

Also, we have been cooking some exciting fresh ways to leverage torch.compile for AMD CPU through the use of AMD ZenDNN PyTorch plugin (zentorch) to speed up even more the kind of workloads we will be discussing after.

While we were able to get early access to this work to test Hugging Face models and libraries and share with you performance, we expect AMD to make it soon available to the community - stay tuned!

According to recent reports, in this section, we present the results from our benchmarking of the two AMD EPYC CPUs: Turin (128 cores) and Genoa (96 cores). For these benchmarks, we utilized the ZenDNN plug-in for PyTorch (zentorch), which provides inference optimizations tailored for deep learning workloads on AMD EPYC CPUs. This plug-in integrates seamlessly with the torch.compile graph compilation flow, enabling multiple passes of graph-level optimizations on the torch.fx graph to achieve further performance acceleration.

It has been revealed that to ensure optimal performance, we used the bfloat16 data type and employed ZenDNN 5.0. We configured multi-instance setups that enable the parallel execution of multiple Meta LLaMA 3.1 8B model instances spawning across all the cores. Each model instance is allocated 32 physical cores per socket, allowing us to leverage the full processing power of the servers for efficient data handling and computational speed.

We ran the benchmarks using two different batch sizes—16 and 32—across five distinct use cases:.

These configurations not only facilitate a comprehensive analysis of how each server performs under varying workloads but also simulate real-world applications of LLMs. Specifically, we plot the decode throughput (excluding the first token) for each use case, to illustrate performance differences.

According to recent reports, throughput results for Meta Llama 3.1 8B, comparing AMD Turin against AMD Genoa. AMD Turin consistently outperforms the AMD Genoa CPUs, achieving approximately 2X higher throughput in most configurations.

Industry observers note that as demonstrated, the AMD EPYC Turin CPU offers a significant boost in performance for AI use cases compared to its predecessor, the AMD Genoa. To enhance reproducibility and streamline the benchmarking process, we utilized optimum-benchmark, which provides a unified framework for efficient benchmarking across various setups. This enabled us to effectively benchmark using the zentorch backend for torch.compile.

Furthermore, we have developed an optimized Dockerfile that will be released soon, along with the benchmarking code. This will facilitate easy deployment and reproduction of our results, ensuring that others can effectively leverage our findings.

You can find more information at AMD Zen Deep Neural Network (ZenDNN).

Fixing Gradient Accumulation

📅 16 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our friends at Unsloth shared an matter regarding gradient accumulation yesterday that is affecting the transformers Trainer.
  • Gradient accumulation is supposed to be mathematically equivalent to full batch training; however, losses did not match between training runs where the setting was toggled on and off.
  • Inside the modeling code of each model, transformers offers a "default" loss function that's the most typically used one for the model's task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our friends at Unsloth shared an matter regarding gradient accumulation yesterday that is affecting the transformers Trainer. The initial report comes from @bnjmn_marie (kudos to him!).

Gradient accumulation is supposed to be mathematically equivalent to full batch training; however, losses did not match between training runs where the setting was toggled on and off.

Inside the modeling code of each model, transformers offers a "default" loss function that's the most typically used one for the model's task. It is determined by what the modeling class should be used for: question answering, token classification, causal LM, masked LM.

This is the default loss function and it was not meant to be customizable: it is only computed when labels and input_ids are passed as inputs to the model, so the user doesn't have to compute the loss. The default loss is useful but is limited by design: for anything different being done, we expect the labels to not be passed directly, and for users to get the logits back from the model and use them to compute the loss outside of the model.

However, the transformers Trainer, as well as many Trainers, heavily leverage these methods because of the simplicity it offers: it is a double-edged sword. Providing a simple API that becomes different as the use-case differs is not a well-thought out API, and we've been caught by surprise ourselves.

In a recent development, to be precise, for gradient accumulation across token-level tasks like causal LM training, the correct loss should be computed by the total loss across all batches in a gradient accumulation step divided by the total number of all non padding tokens in those batches. This is not the same as the average of the per-batch loss values. The fix is quite simple, see the following:.

To address this glitch, we’re changing the way our models and training work in two ways:.

All model that inherit from PreTrainedModel now have a loss_function property, which is determined by either:.

We are working to ship the first change for the most popular models in this PR: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/34191#pullrequestreview-2372725010. Following this, a call for contributions to help propagate this to the rest of the models will be done so that the majority of models is supported by next release.

We are also actively working to ship the second change in this PR: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/34198, which will allow customers to use their own loss function and make use of the number of samples seen per-batch to help with calculating their loss (and will perform the correct loss calculation during gradient accumulation as more models are supported from the prior change).

By tomorrow, you should expect the Trainer to behave correctly with gradient accumulation. Please install from main in order to benefit from the fix then:.

In general, we are very responsive to bug reports submitted to our issue tracker: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues.

In a recent development, this issue has been in Transformers for some time as it's mostly a default that should be updated by the end-user; however, when defaults become non-intuitive, they are bound to be changed. In this instance, we've updated the code and shipped a fix in less than 24 hours, which is what we aim for problems like this one in transformers. Please, come and submit your issues if you have some; this is the only way we can get transformers to improve and fit well within your different use-cases.

The key takeaway is that gradient accumulation can make training with large effective batch sizes much more practical when GPU memory is limited. The numerical details around loss scaling are especially useful for avoiding subtle training bugs.

In a recent development, answer: It has been working from day 1 😀. There is nothing to wait for.

Industry observers note that keras is the time-tested modeling library for JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow. You might have noticed this line in the demo Colab:.

It has to appear before import keras and controls if the model is running on JAX, PyTorch or TensorFlow. Very handy to try your favorite models on JAX with XLA compilation 🚀.

Keras is a modeling library and keras-hub is its collection of pre-trained models. It was previously called KerasNLP and KerasCV. The rename is in progress. It has all the popular pre-trained models (Llama3, Gemma, StableDiffusion, Segment Anything, ...) with their canonical implementation in Keras.

Industry observers note that I mean, "tokenizer included". model.generate() just works on strings:.

If you don't like "batteries included" and want to get to the underlying tokenizer and model, they are easily accessible:.

This could be, for example, image resizing or augmentation for tasks involving images, or text tokenization like here for a text model. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Speech-to-Speech (S2S) is an exciting new project from Hugging Face that combines several advanced models to create a seamless, almost magical experience: you speak, and the system responds with a synthesized voice.

Industry observers note that the project implements a cascaded pipeline leveraging models available through the Transformers library on the Hugging Face hub. The pipeline consists of the following components:.

What's more, S2S has multi-language support! It currently supports English, French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. You can run the pipeline in single-language mode or use the auto flag for automatic language detection. Check out the repo for more details here.

According to recent reports, running Speech-to-Speech requires significant computational resources. Even on a high-end laptop you might encounter latency issues, particularly when using the most advanced models. While a powerful GPU can mitigate these problems, not everyone has the means (or desire!) to set up their own hardware.

Industry observers note that this is where Hugging Face's Inference Endpoints (IE) come into play. Inference Endpoints allow you to rent a virtual machine equipped with a GPU (or other hardware you might need) and pay only for the time your system is running, providing an ideal solution for deploying performance-heavy applications like Speech-to-Speech.

Sources indicate that in this blog post, we’ll guide you step by step to deploy Speech-to-Speech to a Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. This is what we'll cover:.

Inference Endpoints provide a scalable and efficient way to deploy machine learning models. These endpoints allow you to serve models with minimal setup, leveraging a variety of powerful hardware. Inference Endpoints are ideal for deploying applications that require high performance and reliability, without the need to manage underlying infrastructure.

Here's a few key features, and be sure to check out the documentation for more:.

In a recent development, inference Endpoints supports all of the Transformers and Sentence-Transformers tasks, but can also support custom tasks. These are the IE setup options:.

In a recent development, for simpler models, options 1 and 2 are ideal and make deploying with Inference Endpoints super straightforward. However, for a complex pipeline like S2S, you will need the flexibility of option 3: deploying our IE using a custom Docker image.

Industry observers note that this method not only provides more flexibility but also improved performance by optimizing the build process and gathering necessary data. If you’re dealing with complex model pipelines or want to optimize your application deployment, this guide will offer valuable insights.

Industry observers note that to begin creating a custom Docker image, we started by cloning Hugging Face’s default Docker image repository. This serves as a great starting point for deploying machine learning models in inference tasks.

You can check out all of our changes here.

With the repository cloned, the next step was tailoring the image to support our Speech-to-Speech pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that to integrate the project smoothly, we added the speech-to-speech codebase and any required datasets as submodules. This approach offers better version control, ensuring the exact version of the code and data is always available when the Docker image is built.

By including data directly within the Docker container, we avoid having to download it each time the endpoint is instantiated, which significantly reduces startup time and ensures the system is reproducible. The data is stored in a Hugging Face repository, which provides easy tracking and versioning.

Next, we modified the Dockerfile to suit our needs:.

Once the modifications were in place, we built and pushed the custom image to Docker Hub:.

Industry observers note that with the Docker image built and pushed, it’s ready to be used in the Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. By using this pre-built image, the endpoint can launch faster and run more efficiently, as all dependencies and data are pre-packaged within the image.

Industry observers note that using a custom docker image just requires a slightly different configuration, feel free to check out the documentation. We will walk through the approach to do this in both the GUI and the API.

The Model Repository doesn't actually matter since the models are specified and downloaded in the container creation, but Inference Endpoints requires a model, so feel free to pick a slim one of your choice.

You need to specify HF_TOKEN because we need to download gated models in the container creation stage. This won't be necessary if you use models that aren't gated or private.

The current huggingface-inference-toolkit entrypoint uses port 5000 as default, but the inference endpoint expects port 80. You should match this in the Container Port. We already set it in our dockerfile, but beware if making your own from scratch!

The code for it is done on s2s_handler.py in the speech_to_speech library which we use for the client and webservice_starlette.py in thespeech_to_speech_inference_toolkit which we used to build the docker image. Normally, you would only have a custom handler for an endpoint, but since we want to have a really low latency, we also built the webservice to support websocket connections instead of normal requests. This sounds intimidating at first, but the webservice is only 32 lines of code!

This code will run prepare_handler on startup, which will initialize all the models and warm them up. Then, each message will be processed by inference_handler.process_streaming_data.

This method simply receives the audio data from the client, chunks it into small parts for the VAD, and submits it to a queue for processing. Then it checks the output processing queue (the spoken response from the model!) and returns it if there is something. All of the internal processing is handled by Hugging Face's speech_to_speech library.

Industry observers note that the webservice receives and returns audio. But there is still a big missing piece, how do we record and play back the audio? For that, we created a client that connects to the service. The easiest is to divide the analysis in the connection to the webservice and the recording/playing of audio.

In a recent development, initializing the webservice client requires setting a header for all messages with our Hugging Face Token. When initializing the client, we set what we want to do on common messages (open, close, error, message). This will determine what our client does when the server sends it messages.

We can see that the reactions to the messages are straight forward, with the on_message being the only method with more complexity. This method understands when the server is done responding and starts 'listening' back to the user. Otherwise, it puts the data from the server in the playback queue.

The client's audio section has 4 tasks:.

Sources indicate that the audio is recorded on the audio_input_callback method, it simply submits all chunks to a queue. Then, it is sent to the server with the send_audio method. Here, if there is no audio to send, we still submit an empty array in order to receive a response from the server. The responses from the server are handled by the on_message method we saw earlier in the blog. Then, the playback of the audio responses are handled by the audio_output_callback method. Here we only need to ensure that the audio is in the range we expect (We don't want to destroy someone eardrum's because of a faulty package!) and ensure that the size of the output array is what the playback library expects.

Industry News: Releasing Outlines-core 0.1.0: structured generation in Rust and Python

📅 22 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that dottxt and Hugging Face are excited to announce that we have been collaborating on outlines-core, a Rust port of outlines’s core algorithms for structured generation.
  • In a recent development, these improvements should not only improve the performance for existing outlines owners, but also dramatically increase the ways users can incorporate structured generation into their LLM workflows.
  • Industry observers note that structured generation means that your LLM is guaranteed to follow a desired format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that dottxt and Hugging Face are excited to announce that we have been collaborating on outlines-core, a Rust port of outlines’s core algorithms for structured generation. On top of getting reliable output from LLMs with outlines, this Rust port offers several further benefits to users of outlines:.

In a recent development, these improvements should not only improve the performance for existing outlines owners, but also dramatically increase the ways users can incorporate structured generation into their LLM workflows. outlines-core is now public, integrated in outlines, and the version 0.1.0 of the Python bindings are out. You can find the repo here.

Industry observers note that structured generation means that your LLM is guaranteed to follow a desired format. This could be JSON, a Pydantic Model, a regular expression or a context-free grammar. The key is that structured generation forbids the 'wrong' tokens from being generated.

Sources indicate that let’s take an extremely simple example. The LLM should generate a boolean, “true” or “false”. And nothing more. For the sake of illustration, let’s say that LLMs generate characters instead of tokens. So the first character is ", we can just skip the forward pass. For the second, we don’t need to sample from all possible characters. The LLM should just choose between t or f.

According to recent reports, after that, regardless of the path we take, there is only one valid next character. If the LLM chose t as the first character, then it has to follow with r, u and e. And similarly if it chose f it follows with a, l, s, e. And will choose the last " as the final character regardless of the path. There is of course more under the hood, for more in-depth coverage we recommend this dottxt blog and the associated paper on arxiv.

In a recent development, it might not immediately be obvious how amazing structured generation can be. The first use-case many think of is “nice, now my LLM can return valid JSON, so I can treat it as an API and serialize/deserialize JSON reliably”. But that’s just scratching the surface. When you think about it, structure is everywhere, even in places where you least expect it like the GSM8K benchmark.

These are just a few examples of what structured generation enables:.

In a recent development, and, perhaps more surprising, it reduces the sensitivity of evaluations to the specific prompt being used and the number of shots. Apart from the amazing tricks that structure gives you, it’s also more performant. The dottxt blog has many good articles with performance benchmarks.

Probably the first thing that comes to your mind when you hear “rewrite in Rust” is performance. And yes, that’s the case for outlines-core as well. Several key parts are yet to be moved over to Rust, and despite that, we already see an average 2x improvement in compilation speed.

Industry observers note that before the Rust port, Outlines used Numba to accelerate the building of the index. While Numba is fast (the runtime performance is comparable to Rust), the JIT-compilation of the Numba functions added a source of latency during the first run, which was a source of frustration for many customers. Using Rust means we can compile the index building functions ahead of time, adding no latency during the first run. While this was not crucial in a production context (since the first run could anyways be done as part of deployment), it can make a huge difference during the experimentation phase!

One of the main reasons for rewriting Outlines in Rust is the emphasis on safety and reliability that Rust brings to the table. Rust's strong static typing, combined with Rust's ownership model, eliminate entire classes of bugs, such as null pointer dereferences and data races in concurrent code. This leads to more robust and secure software.

In the context of Outlines, safety is crucial. Structured generation often involves complex data structures and manipulations, especially when dealing with high-performance inference engines. By leveraging Rust's safety guarantees, we reduce the risk of runtime errors and undefined behaviors that can arise from memory mismanagement.

Additionally, Rust's compile-time checks encourage developers to write cleaner and more maintainable code. This improves the current codebase and makes future development more efficient. New contributors can onboard more swiftly, and the code is easier to audit and verify for correctness.

It has been revealed that outlines was designed to do more than providing the core algorithms for structured generation. Among other things, it includes integrations to other libraries like transformers which mean the library packs many dependencies. Separating the core algorithms from the Outlines library means that other libraries wishing to include structured generation can do so by importing a very lightweight library. So we can imagine in the near future libraries such as transformers and llama-cpp-python integrating structured generation directly. This allows the dottxt team to focus on the core algorithms.

According to recent reports, most of LLM training is written in Python, but inference is slightly different. It happens on many different devices, on specialized servers and is written in a range of programming languages. This is why portability also matters for structured generation. By having the core functionality of outlines written in rust, we can now create bindings to other languages.

Sources indicate that for example, this port makes the integration into the text-generation-inference much smoother. TGI’s server logic is written in Rust, and we want to avoid having to call Python code as much as we possibly can. It also means libraries like mistral.rs or models implemented using candle can benefit from Outlines’s performance and capabilities.

According to recent reports, in the future we plan to explore bindings to JS/TS, allowing outlines to be used in transformers-js. Or potentially Swift bindings, making outlines natively usable on Apple devices. But for now the focus is going to be on the Python bindings, and continuing to make outlines-core’s feature set complete by expanding support for the JSON Schema specification.

According to recent reports, do you like working with structured generation, parsers, making LLMs output only valid JSON? Star the library, tweet about it, join in and contribute! Share your work on Twitter, and with dottxt’s and Hugging Face's community.

Recent findings suggest that webGPU is a new web standard for accelerated graphics and compute. The API enables web developers to use the underlying system's GPU to carry out high-performance computations directly in the browser. WebGPU is the successor to WebGL and provides significantly better performance, because it allows for more direct interaction with modern GPUs. Lastly, it supports general-purpose GPU computations, which makes it just perfect for machine learning!

As of October 2024, global WebGPU support is around 70% (according to caniuse.com), meaning some users may not be able to use the API.

If the following demos do not work in your browser, you may need to enable it using a feature flag:.

Thanks to our collaboration with ONNX Runtime Web, enabling WebGPU acceleration is as simple as setting device: 'webgpu' when loading a model. Let's see some examples!

Example: Compute text embeddings on WebGPU (demo).

Example: Perform automatic speech recognition with OpenAI whisper on WebGPU (demo).

Example: Perform image classification with MobileNetV4 on WebGPU (demo).

Sources indicate that before Transformers.js v3, we used the quantized option to specify whether to use a quantized (q8) or full-precision (fp32) variant of the model by setting quantized to true or false, respectively. Now, we've added the ability to select from a much larger list with the dtype parameter.

The list of available quantizations depends on the model, but some common ones are: full-precision ("fp32"), half-precision ("fp16"), 8-bit ("q8", "int8", "uint8"), and 4-bit ("q4", "bnb4", "q4f16").

(e.g., mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-xsmall-v1).

Example: Run Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct in 4-bit quantization (demo).

According to recent reports, some encoder-decoder models, like Whisper or Florence-2, are extremely sensitive to quantization settings: especially of the encoder. For this reason, we added the ability to select per-module dtypes, which can be done by providing a mapping from module name to dtype.

Example: Run Florence-2 on WebGPU (demo).

Recent findings suggest that this release increases the total number of supported architectures to 120 (see full list), spanning a wide range of input modalities and tasks. Notable newly introduced names include: Phi-3, Gemma & Gemma 2, LLaVa, Moondream, Florence-2, MusicGen, Sapiens, Depth Pro, PyAnnote, and RT-DETR.

It has been revealed that as part of the release, we've published 25 upcoming example projects and templates, primarily focused on showcasing WebGPU support! This includes demos like Phi-3.5 WebGPU and Whisper WebGPU, as shown below.

We're in the process of moving all our example projects and demos to https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js-examples, so stay tuned for updates on this!

As of today's release, the community has converted over 1200 models to be compatible with Transformers.js! You can find the full list of available models here.

If you'd like to convert your own models or fine-tunes, you can use our conversion script as follows:.

After uploading the generated files to the Hugging Face Hub, remember to add the transformers.js tag so others can easily find and use your model!

Transformers.js v3 is now compatible with the three most popular server-side JavaScript runtimes:.

Finally, we're delighted to announce that Transformers.js will now be published under the official Hugging Face organization on NPM as @huggingface/transformers (instead of @xenova/transformers, which was used for v1 and v2).

We've also moved the repository to the official Hugging Face organization on GitHub (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js), which will be our newly introduced home — come say hi! We look forward to hearing your feedback, responding to your complications, and reviewing your PRs!

It has been revealed that this is a significant milestone and we're extremely grateful to the community for helping us achieve this long-term goal! None of this would be possible without all of you… thank you! 🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are pleased to announce our partnership with Protect AI, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

According to recent reports, protect AI is a company founded with a mission to create a safer AI-powered world. They are developing powerful tools, namely Guardian, to ensure that the rapid pace of AI innovation can continue without compromising security.

Our decision to partner with Protect AI stems from their community driven approach to security, active support of open source, and expertise in all things security x AI.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

To share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating Guardian in our scanner suite.

It has been revealed that pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that Guardian catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Knowledge Base for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥.

While integrating Guardian as a third-party scanner, we have used this as an opportunity to revamp our frontend to display scan results. Here is what it now looks like:.

Industry observers note that as you can see from the screenshot, there's nothing you have to do to benefit from this! All public model repositories will be scanned by Guardian automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

In a recent development, note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have over 1 million model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.

Sources indicate that in this blog post we share the journey of releasing CinePile 2.0, a significantly improved version of our long video QA dataset. The improvements in the new dataset rely on a new approach that we coined adversarial dataset refinement.

We're excited to share both CinePile 2.0 and our adversarial refinement method implementation, which we believe can strengthen many existing datasets and directly be part of future dataset creation pipelines.

If you are mainly interested in the adversarial refinement method, you can jump directly to the Adversarial Refinement section.

In May 2024, we launched CinePile, a long video QA dataset with about 300,000 training samples and 5,000 test samples.

The first release stood out from other datasets in two aspects:.

Industry observers note that part of the secret sauce behind it is that it relies on movie clips from YouTube and Q&A distilled from precise audio descriptions designed for visually impaired audiences. These descriptions offer rich context beyond basic visuals (e.g., "What color is the car?"), helping us create more complex questions.

It has been revealed that to automate question creation, we first built question templates by inspecting existing datasets like MovieQA and TVQA. We clustered the questions in these datasets using a textual similarity model WhereIsAI/UAE-Large-V1 and then prompted GPT-4 with 10 random examples from each cluster to generate a question template and a prototypical question for each:.

It has been revealed that since templates aren't always relevant to every movie clip, we used Gemini 1.0 Pro to select the most appropriate ones for each scene. Next, we feed a language model the scene's text, selected template names (e.g., "Physical Possession"), sample questions, and a system prompt to create scene-specific questions. A well-designed prompt helps the model focus on the entire scene, generating deeper questions while avoiding superficial ones. We found that:.

Using this approach, we generate approximately 32 questions per video. Prior to releasing CinePile, we implemented several mechanisms to ensure the quality of the dataset/benchmark that we cover in the next section.

While our process typically generates well-formed, answerable questions, some turn out to be trivial or rely on basic concepts that don't require watching the clip. To address this, we used several large language models (LLMs) to identify and filter three types of issues:.

Through continued use of the benchmark by our team and the broader community, we identified several areas for improvement that drove us to consider CinePile 2.0.

For CinePile's second release, we worked together with Hugging Face (following their successful experimentation with fine-tuning Video Llava 7B on CinePile) to identify and prioritize several areas of improvement.

While the degeneracy filtering was useful in CinePile 1.0, it had several limitations:.

In a recent development, to address these issues, we introduced a upcoming Adversarial Refinement pipeline that helps improve weak questions rather than simply discarding them. This approach can be more easily applied at scale. Throughout this post, we'll refer to the model(s) that identify degenerate questions (using only the question and answer choices, without visual or dialogue information) as the "Deaf-Blind LLM.".

The Adversarial Refinement pipeline aims to modify questions or answers until a Deaf-Blind LLM cannot easily predict the correct answer. Here's how it works:.

Recent findings suggest that in this release, we're publishing both our adversarial refinement pipeline and the code for identifying weak questions. The complete implementation, including all prompts, is available in our public repository.

This gap highlights the value of CinePile's new release as a benchmark for measuring progress toward more sophisticated visual understanding.

AI-generated images are becoming a common part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product illustrations, landing pages, blog posts, and digital interfaces. However, generating an image is only one part of the process. Before publishing it, developers need to ensure that the image loads swiftly, displays correctly across devices, and maintains its visual quality.

Large image files can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay the appearance of crucial content. These problems can affect user experience and website performance, particularly on mobile devices and slower internet connections.

A reliable image optimization workflow helps address these challenges. By selecting appropriate dimensions, choosing efficient image formats, automating image processing, and implementing responsive delivery, developers can improve loading performance without sacrificing visual quality.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques and development tools.

According to recent reports, images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. Uploading large, unoptimized images can make pages slower and increase the amount of data visitors need to download.

Several common problems contribute to poor image performance:.

Large files take longer to download.

Incorrect dimensions waste bandwidth on smaller screens.

Inefficient formats increase file sizes.

Missing image dimensions can cause unexpected layout shifts.

Poor responsive configuration can make browsers download unnecessarily large images.

Incorrect loading priorities can delay notable visual content.

These concerns can affect Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how swiftly the largest visible content element appears.

For developers, image optimization should therefore be part of the website development workflow rather than a final task performed immediately before publication.

Industry observers note that before optimizing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small interface graphic.

For example, a website might use the following dimensions:.

Sources indicate that these dimensions are examples rather than fixed requirements. The appropriate size depends on the website layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

When preparing source visuals, developers can explore different AI image generation options and consider how the generated images will fit their intended layouts.

According to recent reports, once the image is ready, keep a high-quality master file. This allows developers to create smaller versions for different screen sizes without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Avoid enlarging small images unnecessarily because upscaling can introduce blur and visible artifacts.

Choosing the right format can reduce image size while preserving acceptable visual quality.

Three commonly used formats are AVIF, WebP, and JPEG.

In a recent development, AVIF: Often provides efficient compression for photographs and detailed illustrations. It can significantly reduce file sizes, although encoding may take longer.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation. It offers broad browser support and is suitable for many website images.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and situations where compatibility with older software or systems is vital.

PNG is appropriate for certain lossless graphics, screenshots, and images that require transparency. However, it can produce unnecessarily large files when used for photographic content.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare file sizes and inspect visual quality before selecting the final output.

A practical approach is to generate AVIF and WebP versions and provide a JPEG fallback where necessary.

Manually resizing and converting images becomes time-consuming when a website contains dozens or hundreds of visual assets.

Automation makes the process more consistent. Developers can use Sharp, a Node.js image-processing library, to resize images, convert formats, and generate multiple versions from a single source file.

Next, create a file named build-images.mjs:.

The script creates multiple image sizes in both WebP and AVIF formats.

The quality settings are starting points, not universal recommendations. Developers should adjust them after checking the resulting file sizes and visual details.

This approach is particularly useful for content-heavy websites, product catalogs, and applications that publish images regularly.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on the visitor's screen and the space available in the layout.

HTML provides two vital attributes for this purpose: srcset and sizes.

The srcset attribute lists the available image files and their widths. The sizes attribute describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes.

In this example, the image is expected to occupy approximately 720 pixels on wider screens and nearly the full viewport width on smaller screens.

The browser uses this information to choose an appropriate image candidate.

In a recent development, one common mistake is setting sizes="100vw" for an image that occupies only a small part of the page. This can encourage the browser to download a larger file than necessary.

Always ensure that the sizes attribute reflects the actual website layout.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide multiple image formats and a fallback option.

The browser selects a supported format, while the img element provides the fallback image and alternative text.

Developers should verify that every referenced file exists and that its dimensions match the intended layout.

The picture element can also support different crops for desktop and mobile devices. This is useful when a wide banner needs a separate composition for smaller screens.

Images without defined dimensions can cause content to move while the browser loads the file. This behavior contributes to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Including width and height attributes helps browsers reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

For responsive layouts, developers can use CSS:.

This allows images to scale within their containers while maintaining their proportions.

Images below the initial viewport can generally use native lazy loading:.

However, the main hero image should not normally be lazy-loaded when it is responsible for LCP. Delaying an important above-the-fold image can make the page appear slower.

Where appropriate, developers can use fetchpriority="high" for the main image to help the browser prioritize its download.

The correct strategy depends on the image's position and importance within the page.

Industry observers note that image optimization involves more than file size and dimensions. Developers should also consider accessibility, file organization, and metadata.

Industry observers note that alternative text helps people using screen readers understand meaningful images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page.

Decorative images that provide no useful information should generally use an empty alt attribute.

Industry observers note that file names should also be descriptive. Names such as home-office-sunrise.webp are easier to understand and maintain than generic names such as image-final-v3.png.

Metadata requires additional consideration. Image-processing tools may remove metadata by default to reduce file size. This can include information that a project needs to preserve, depending on its requirements.

Before removing metadata, developers should review whether the website or client requires attribution, provenance information, or other embedded details.

After implementing an optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Chrome DevTools provides useful information about image requests.

Open Developer Tools and select the Network panel.

Resize the viewport or use device emulation.

Check whether the browser downloads appropriately sized images.

Developers can also inspect the image selected by the browser through the console:.

This returns the current image URL selected for that element.

For websites with multiple images, inspect the relevant elements individually.

Finally, run an audit using Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. These tools can identify issues involving oversized images, image formats, loading priorities, and other performance factors.

Recent findings suggest that image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, JavaScript, and third-party scripts can also influence loading speed.

Several mistakes can reduce the effectiveness of an image optimization workflow:.

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one format always produces the smallest file.

Omitting the sizes attribute from responsive images.

Forgetting width and height attributes.

Lazy-loading vital above-the-fold images.

Applying excessive compression and damaging visual details.

Generating unnecessary image variations.

Testing only on desktop devices.

Removing metadata without checking project requirements.

Measuring file size without inspecting the final visual quality.

A consistent testing process helps identify these problems before they affect visitors.

According to recent reports, no. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but the results depend on the image, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best way to choose an appropriate option.

Industry observers note that four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

It has been revealed that yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

According to recent reports, no. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Vital images near the top of the page should generally load promptly.

It has been revealed that the fundamental techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, AI-generated visuals may contain complex textures, gradients, and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design and make it easier to create custom visual content. However, efficient delivery requires more than exporting an image and uploading it to a website.

Developers should choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive image delivery. Including image dimensions helps prevent layout shifts, while appropriate loading priorities can improve the experience for visitors.

By testing images across different devices and reviewing their actual performance, development teams can maintain visual quality while reducing unnecessary downloads.

A repeatable optimization workflow makes it easier to publish upcoming visuals without sacrificing website speed, accessibility, or reliability.

Introducing SynthID Text

📅 23 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face
