In a recent development, legacy applications often support critical business operations, but keeping them running can become increasingly difficult. Outdated infrastructure, growing technical debt, security vulnerabilities, and limited integration capabilities can make these systems expensive to maintain and harder to adapt to changing business needs.

Modernizing them involves more than upgrading technology. You need to understand what the existing application does, identify which components need improvement, and manage the transition without disrupting essential operations.

This 10-point legacy application modernization checklist walks you through the process, from assessing your existing systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, testing applications, and measuring results.

Legacy application modernization is the process of updating existing software applications, their architecture, infrastructure, or underlying technologies to meet current business and technical requirements.

Depending on the application's condition, modernization may involve moving it to a new platform, improving its code, redesigning its architecture, or replacing it with a new solution.

The goal is to improve performance, security, scalability, maintainability, and the application's ability to support future business requirements.

In a recent development, modernization isn't necessarily the same as cloud migration. Moving an application from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud changes where it runs, but it may leave its underlying architecture and technical limitations unchanged.

An organization can modernize an application without moving it to the cloud or combine both approaches as part of a larger transformation.

Use this checklist to track the ten essential steps involved in modernizing legacy applications.

1. Define modernization goals: Identify business problems and establish measurable success criteria.

2. Assess existing applications: Review infrastructure, technical debt, code quality, and performance limitations.

3. Map application dependencies: Document critical workflows, integrations, and business rules.

Industry observers note that 4. Choose a modernization strategy: Select an approach based on business value, cost, complexity, and risk.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Develop a roadmap and budget: Prioritize activities, estimate costs, assign responsibilities, and establish milestones.

Sources indicate that 6. Plan architecture and security: Design the target environment and address security, compliance, and availability requirements.

Recent findings suggest that 7. Prepare data migration: Plan data transfer, integration changes, and validation procedures.

8. Modernize incrementally: Validate the approach with a pilot and implement changes in manageable phases.

It has been revealed that 9. Test and deploy: Verify functionality, performance, security, and data integrity before production rollout.

10. Monitor and optimize: Measure results, support users, and continuously improve the modernized application.

Let's examine what each step involves and how to determine whether you're ready to proceed.

Before selecting technologies or planning development work, identify what the modernization initiative needs to achieve.

Clear business objectives help prioritize investments, guide technical decisions, and establish whether the project delivers meaningful improvements.

Start by examining the problems affecting your application's performance, reliability, or business value.

For example, a legacy order management system might still process transactions reliably but require extensive manual work whenever the business adds a new sales channel.

In this situation, improving integration capabilities may be more valuable than replacing the entire application.

An application's age alone doesn't justify a major technology investment. Whether legacy modernization makes sense for your business depends on the problems the existing system creates, the cost of maintaining it, and whether smaller improvements could resolve those concerns.

Once you've identified the problems, translate them into measurable objectives.

According to recent reports, if slow performance is the primary concern, establish a target for response times or transaction processing speed. If maintenance expenses are rising, determine what reduction in operating costs would justify the investment.

Relevant key performance indicators (KPIs) may include:.

These baseline measurements will help determine whether the changes deliver the expected results.

Completion check: You have a documented business case identifying the problems to address, expected outcomes, measurable KPIs, and stakeholders responsible for approving success.

A legacy application assessment provides a clear picture of your current technology environment.

Without this assessment, teams may underestimate project complexity, overlook critical components, or choose a modernization approach that doesn't address the application's actual limitations.

Begin by creating an inventory of your applications and their supporting technologies.

Document each application's purpose, business owner, primary users, operating environment, programming languages, frameworks, databases, and infrastructure requirements.

Also identify software versions, third-party dependencies, licensing restrictions, and components approaching or past their end-of-support dates.

If your organization operates several legacy applications, use a consistent assessment framework. This makes it easier to compare their business importance, technical condition, and modernization urgency.

Review the application's codebase to identify problems that make maintenance and development difficult.

Look for tightly coupled components, duplicated logic, outdated libraries, insufficient automated tests, and undocumented configurations.

Pay particular attention to areas where small modifications regularly cause unexpected problems elsewhere in the system.

For example, if payment processing, inventory management, and customer records share tightly connected code, modifying one function could require extensive testing across the entire application.

Your infrastructure assessment should also cover hardware limitations, database compatibility, backup capabilities, operating systems, and unsupported dependencies.

Analyze how the application performs during normal operations and periods of increased demand.

Review response times, database queries, resource utilization, transaction volumes, and recurring failures.

Existing monitoring data and incident records can reveal problems that aren't immediately visible during routine use.

Determine whether performance limitations originate from inefficient application code, infrastructure capacity, database design, or external dependencies.

This distinction matters because adding computing resources won't necessarily resolve problems caused by poor application logic.

Completion check: You have an application inventory and technical assessment report documenting major components, technical debt, operational risks, and performance limitations.

Sources indicate that legacy applications rarely operate independently. They exchange data with other systems, support interconnected business processes, and often contain business rules that aren't fully documented.

Understanding these dependencies is essential because changing one component can affect several other applications or workflows.

Document the processes that rely on the application, including the steps owners follow, the data they need, and the expected outcomes.

Work with business customers, application owners, operations teams, and developers familiar with the system.

Identify processes that cannot tolerate significant interruption, such as payment processing, order fulfillment, customer authentication, or financial reporting.

Don't overlook activities that happen less frequently. Month-end financial reports, annual calculations, and scheduled data exchanges may depend on functionality that isn't exercised during everyday operations.

Map how the application communicates with databases, APIs, third-party services, and other internal systems.

Include scheduled jobs, file transfers, message queues, authentication services, and reporting tools.

Some legacy applications contain years of accumulated business logic.

Rules for pricing, approvals, calculations, or customer eligibility may exist only in source code, database procedures, or undocumented workflows.

Identify these rules before modifying the underlying implementation.

Where possible, create automated tests that capture existing expected behavior. These tests can help verify that the modernized application preserves required functionality.

Completion check: Critical workflows, system dependencies, integrations, and business rules are documented and reviewed by the relevant business and technical owners.

The appropriate modernization strategy depends on the application's technical condition, business importance, budget, and future requirements.

Industry observers note that not every application needs to be rebuilt. Some systems require targeted improvements, while others may be better replaced or retired.

Common legacy application modernization strategies include:.

Different applications within the same organization may require different approaches.

Evaluate each option against your technical constraints and business requirements.

Consider implementation effort, expected benefits, ongoing maintenance costs, required expertise, and potential disruption.

Recent findings suggest that for example, replatforming may be suitable for an application that operates reliably but depends on aging infrastructure. Rearchitecting may be necessary when tightly coupled components prevent independent updates or scaling.

A complete rebuild requires particular caution. Recreating undocumented functionality can be expensive, and important business rules may be lost if the existing system hasn't been thoroughly assessed.

The right strategy should solve the identified problems without introducing unnecessary cost or complexity.

Completion check: Each application has a selected modernization strategy, documented rationale, estimated effort, and an approved decision on whether to modernize, retain, replace, or retire it.

Once you've selected a modernization approach, convert it into an actionable plan.

Your roadmap should establish what will change, in what order, who will be responsible, and how progress will be evaluated.

Prioritize modernization work according to business value, technical complexity, urgency, and dependencies.

Applications with unsupported components or significant security risks may require early attention. However, starting with the most complex application isn't always the best choice.

A smaller, lower-risk application can provide an opportunity to validate tools, workflows, and team capabilities before modernizing more critical systems.

According to recent reports, dependencies also affect the sequence. For example, a shared authentication service may need to be updated before applications that rely on it can be migrated.

Prepare a budget covering the full modernization process rather than development alone.

Relevant cost categories include:.

Compare upfront implementation expenses with expected operating costs over time.

A modernization approach with a lower initial cost may still require significant ongoing maintenance.

Allow contingency for unexpected issues, particularly when legacy documentation is incomplete or system dependencies remain uncertain.

Divide the project into phases with defined deliverables and approval requirements.

Assign responsible owners for architecture, development, security, data migration, testing, and business acceptance.

Establish how project risks will be reported and who can approve changes to scope, budget, or deployment schedules.

Keep the roadmap adaptable. Findings from pilot implementations or migration rehearsals may require changes to the original blueprint.

Completion check: Your modernization roadmap includes prioritized activities, estimated costs, responsible owners, dependencies, milestones, and approval checkpoints.

The target architecture determines how the modernized application will operate, scale, integrate with other systems, and remain maintainable.

Security and compliance requirements should be incorporated into the design from the beginning.

Choose an architecture that fits the application's actual requirements.

Possible approaches include a modular monolith, service-oriented architecture, microservices, or event-driven components.

In a recent development, microservices aren't automatically the best option. Although they allow independent deployment and scaling of components, they also introduce complexity in communication, monitoring, deployment, and data management.

For smaller applications or tightly integrated business processes, a well-structured modular architecture may be easier to maintain.

Document architectural decisions covering application components, data storage, interfaces, infrastructure requirements, and operational responsibilities.

Identify security weaknesses that should be resolved during modernization.

Review authentication, authorization, encryption, secrets management, logging, and access to sensitive information.

Evaluate third-party dependencies and establish processes for vulnerability scanning, patching, and security testing.

Regulatory and contractual requirements should also influence the target design.

Depending on the organization, these may include data privacy obligations, retention requirements, audit controls, or restrictions on where information can be stored.

Security controls should be applied throughout development and deployment rather than added shortly before release.

Define how the application will remain available and recover from failures.

Establish recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs) based on business requirements.

Initiative backup procedures, restoration testing, appropriate redundancy, and monitoring for critical components.

Validate that the target environment can support the required availability and recovery objectives.

Completion check: The target architecture has documented design decisions, security controls, compliance requirements, availability objectives, and recovery procedures.

Data migration is one of the most sensitive stages of legacy application modernization.

Legacy databases may contain inconsistent records, outdated formats, duplicated information, or relationships that newer systems handle differently.

A migration strategy needs to explain how data will be transferred, validated, and made available without compromising business operations.

Begin by reviewing the quality and structure of existing data.

Identify missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, obsolete fields, and relationships that could create migration problems.

Document how existing data structures correspond to the target system.

For example, a legacy customer database might store contact details in a single field, while the fresh application requires separate fields for email addresses and phone numbers.

The migration process needs defined transformation rules to handle these differences.

Determine which records must be migrated, archived, retained for compliance, or excluded.

Choose a migration approach based on data volume, application availability requirements, and acceptable downtime.

Depending on the system, this may involve a scheduled migration during a maintenance window, staged transfers, or synchronization between old and upcoming environments.

Identify integrations that will need modification.

Where applications exchange information through APIs, files, or messaging systems, verify that the modernized implementation supports the required data formats and business behavior.

If the legacy and modernized applications will operate simultaneously, define how data updates will be synchronized between them.

Test the migration process using representative datasets before transferring production data.

Validate record counts, field values, relationships, and critical business calculations.

For sensitive or business-critical information, use appropriate reconciliation methods, including integrity checks where applicable.

Document how inconsistencies will be identified and resolved.

Also establish what happens if migration fails or the application needs to return to its previous environment.

Completion check: Data mapping rules are approved, migration rehearsals have been completed, and reconciliation procedures can verify data accuracy.

Modernizing an entire application in a single major release can increase project risk, particularly when the system supports critical business operations.

An incremental approach allows teams to validate decisions, identify problems earlier, and limit the impact of failures.

Select a manageable component or workload to validate your modernization approach.

The pilot should test an notable assumption, such as whether the target platform supports the application, whether a legacy integration can be replaced, or whether an architectural change improves performance.

Define success criteria before implementation.

A useful pilot should provide evidence that the approach is technically feasible and that the team can manage its operational requirements.

Use the findings to improve estimates, identify missing skills, and refine the broader implementation plan.

Divide the application into manageable migration or development units where its architecture allows.

One approach is the Strangler Fig pattern, which gradually replaces legacy functionality while the remaining parts of the original application continue operating.

For example, an organization might modernize customer notifications first, followed by reporting and then core transaction processing.

This can reduce the risks associated with replacing an entire system at once.

However, incremental modernization also requires careful coordination. Temporary integrations, duplicated components, and parallel systems can introduce complexity.

Each phase should have defined boundaries, validation requirements, and completion criteria.

Establish repeatable processes for developing, testing, and deploying application changes.

Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines can automate builds, execute tests, and promote approved changes through environments.

Use version control, consistent configuration management, and infrastructure as code where appropriate.

Include security and quality checks in the delivery process to reduce the risk of introducing defects during frequent releases.

Completion check: The pilot has validated the selected approach, implementation is divided into manageable phases, and repeatable build, test, and deployment processes are established.

Modernization isn't complete when the new application runs successfully in a development environment.

It must perform the required business functions, communicate correctly with connected systems, and meet operational expectations before production rollout.

Develop a testing plan based on the application's critical workflows and identified risks.

Automate repeatable tests where practical, especially for critical business processes.

Compare results against the performance baselines and acceptance criteria established earlier.

Business owners should verify that the modernized application supports their actual workflows.

User acceptance testing (UAT) should include routine operations, exception handling, reporting requirements, and tasks that depend on specialized business knowledge.

Use representative migrated data during testing.

Confirm that critical records, calculations, and reports remain accurate after the transition.

Resolve issues affecting essential operations before approving production deployment.

Prepare a documented deployment blueprint outlining the sequence of activities, responsible teams, communication channels, and expected service interruptions.

Choose a deployment method appropriate for the application, such as a phased rollout, canary release, or scheduled cutover.

Establish measurable conditions that would stop deployment or trigger a rollback.

Recent findings suggest that rollback planning must account for data changes made after cutover. Restoring an earlier application version doesn't automatically restore database consistency, especially if new transactions have already been processed.

Rehearse deployment and recovery procedures in a suitable non-production environment.

Completion check: Required tests have passed, business owners have approved acceptance criteria, and deployment, cutover, and recovery procedures have been validated.

The initial deployment marks the beginning of ongoing operation rather than the end of modernization.

The application needs continued monitoring and maintenance to ensure that expected improvements are sustained.

Compare post-modernization results against the baseline established at the beginning of the project.

Track metrics linked to your business objectives, such as application availability, maintenance costs, response times, deployment frequency, security vulnerabilities, and user satisfaction.

Use monitoring tools, logs, traces, and alerts to identify problems that may not be visible through basic availability checks.

Review performance after deployment and at agreed intervals to determine whether the modernization initiative is meeting its objectives.

Technical improvements may introduce changes to established workflows.

Provide relevant training, updated documentation, and support resources for users and operational teams.

Ensure that administrators and developers understand the fresh architecture, deployment processes, monitoring tools, and incident response procedures.

Collect user feedback to identify usability issues or missing functionality.

Use production data and operational feedback to guide further improvements.

Optimization may involve updating dependencies, improving database queries, adjusting infrastructure capacity, strengthening security controls, or simplifying application components.

Once replacement functionality is stable and approved, begin decommissioning components that are no longer needed.

Before retirement, confirm that dependent applications have been migrated, necessary records are retained, and archival or compliance obligations have been met.

Removing unused infrastructure and software can reduce maintenance costs and unnecessary security exposure.

Completion check: Monitoring and support responsibilities are established, modernization KPIs are reviewed, and unused legacy components have an approved retirement strategy.

Organizations without the internal resources to manage legacy modernization may need support from an external software development organization.

Depending on the project, a development partner can assist with application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, system integration, data migration, and implementation.

Companies offering custom software development and application modernization services include:.

Idea Maker: Provides custom software development and legacy application modernization services, including application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, and cloud migration.

ScienceSoft: Offers custom software development, legacy software modernization, application reengineering, cloud migration, and system integration services.

Itransition: Provides custom application development, legacy application modernization, system integration, software migration, and post-modernization support.

Simform: Offers digital product engineering, software modernization, cloud and platform engineering, and data integration services.

These are examples of providers rather than a ranked comparison.

When evaluating a development partner, consider their experience with your existing technology stack, ability to handle complex integrations, approach to data security, and experience delivering projects with similar requirements.

Ask prospective providers how they assess legacy systems, manage migration risks, preserve critical business logic, and validate application functionality before deployment.

The main steps are defining business goals, assessing existing applications, mapping dependencies, choosing a modernization strategy, developing a roadmap, designing the target architecture, planning data migration, implementing changes, testing and deploying, and continuously optimizing the application.

The exact sequence may vary depending on the application's complexity and business requirements.

Start by evaluating the application's business value, technical condition, dependencies, and future requirements.

Rehosting or replatforming may be sufficient when the application functions well and infrastructure is the primary concern.

Refactoring or rearchitecting may be necessary when code quality or architectural limitations affect maintainability and scalability.

Rebuilding or replacing becomes an option when the existing implementation no longer meets business needs or would be too costly to maintain.

Compare expected benefits, implementation costs, risks, and ongoing maintenance requirements before making a decision.

Common risks include undocumented dependencies, data loss or corruption, unexpected downtime, security vulnerabilities, integration failures, and loss of essential business functionality.

Projects may also experience delays or budget overruns when technical complexity is underestimated.

These risks can be reduced through early assessment, phased implementation, migration rehearsals, comprehensive testing, and validated recovery procedures.

The timeline depends on the application's size, architecture, technical debt, data complexity, integrations, and selected modernization approach.

A limited rehosting or refactoring project generally requires less effort than rebuilding a large application or modernizing several interconnected systems.

A reliable estimate requires an initial technical assessment. A pilot or proof of concept can help validate assumptions about implementation effort and potential challenges.

Measure success against the business and technical objectives established before implementation.

Relevant indicators include application performance, availability, maintenance costs, security improvements, deployment speed, and user satisfaction.

For example, if reducing maintenance effort was the primary goal, lower support costs and faster resolution of application issues may be more meaningful than infrastructure performance alone.

Modernization success should be evaluated over time rather than only immediately after deployment.

Legacy application modernization works best when it follows a structured strategy based on business needs and the realities of existing technology.

The ten steps in this checklist cover the key decisions and activities involved, from assessing legacy systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, validating functionality, and maintaining the resulting application.

Careful dependency mapping, realistic planning, incremental implementation, and thorough testing help reduce risks throughout the transition.

Industry observers note that start by assessing your existing applications and defining what modernization needs to achieve. Those findings will help you identify which systems deserve attention, where to invest resources, and how to approach modernization without introducing unnecessary complexity.

Industry News: SmolVLM - small yet mighty Vision Language Model

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this blog post introduces SmolVLM, a 2B VLM, SOTA for its memory footprint.
  • This year has seen a boom in multimodal AI with many large vision language models released.
  • In this blog post, we introduce SmolVLM, a new family of 2B small vision language models that can be used commercially and deployed to smaller local setups, with completely open training pipelines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this blog post introduces SmolVLM, a 2B VLM, SOTA for its memory footprint. SmolVLM is small, fast, memory-efficient, and fully open-source. All model checkpoints, VLM datasets, training recipes and tools are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

This year has seen a boom in multimodal AI with many large vision language models released. The trends were to initially scale up compute, later scale up the data diversity by generating synthetic data with large models, and, recently, scale down to make these models more efficient. Small open models allow local deployment to browser or edge devices, cut inference costs, and enable user customization. Some notable examples of these models include PaliGemma 3B, moondream2, and Qwen2VL.

In this blog post, we introduce SmolVLM, a new family of 2B small vision language models that can be used commercially and deployed to smaller local setups, with completely open training pipelines.

We release three models: SmolVLM-Base, which can be used for downstream fine-tuning, SmolVLM-Synthetic, the fine-tuned variant on synthetic data, and SmolVLM Instruct, the fine-tuned instruction variant, which can be used out of the box for interactive end-user applications.

Sources indicate that this release comes with open-source models integrated into transformers, a demo built on SmolVLM Instruct, and a supervised fine-tuning script. We have used the datasets previously used for Idefics3: the Cauldron and Docmatix, which are also fully open-source.

Recent findings suggest that the Main Building: Located at the center of the complex, the main building features intricate tile work with traditional Thai motifs that cover every inch of the structure. This includes patterns such as dragons, mythical creatures, flowers, and geometric shapes. The roofline has an elaborate design featuring multiple layers of tiles adorned with gold accents.

Towers & Spires: There are several towers within the Grand Palace including the Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya National Museum Tower which houses exhibits on Thai culture and heritage. Another notable tower is the Wat Yai Chai Mongkol Tower where you can find beautiful murals depicting scenes from Buddhist mythology.

Architecture Style: The architectural style combines elements of Hindu and Khmer styles seen commonly throughout Southeast Asia. You'll notice influences like stupas (dome-shaped structures), lotus flower carvings, and ornate details typical of these regions' religious buildings.

Recent findings suggest that visitor Experience: While exploring the Grand Palace, visitors should be aware of certain rules due to security measures taken by authorities. These include no photography inside certain areas or using flashbulbs outside. Additionally, there may be queues during peak tourist seasons so plan accordingly if you're traveling here.

By following these guidelines, your trip will undoubtedly enhance both your understanding of Thailand’s rich historical tapestry and personal enjoyment!

According to recent reports, for SmolVLM, we closely followed the architecture from Idefics3, to the point that we use the same implementation in transformers. There are, however a few key differences:.

We present benchmarks for the tasks we mention in training details.

It has been revealed that smolVLM provides the best memory usage among the existing suite of vision language models in transformers. This allows it to run efficiently on-device, such as a laptop! You can see above the GPU memory usage in GBs for each model, running inference with one or two input images, and using the same images and text prompts in all tests. SmolVLM's efficiency in image encoding is built into the model. SmolVLM encodes each 384x384 image patch to 81 tokens. This results in SmolVLM encoding our test prompt and a single image in 1.2k tokens, whereas Qwen2-VL uses 16k tokens. This also explains why the memory consumption increases so much for 2 images with Qwen and InternVL. In contrast, the increase is much more moderate for SmolVLM and PaliGemma, which use a similar approach.

SmolVLM's tiny memory footprint also implies that it requires far fewer computations to prefill the model and generate. Compared to Qwen2-VL, the prefill throughput is 3.3 to 4.5 times faster, and the generation throughput is 7.5 to 16 times faster.

Given SmolVLM's long context and the possibility of tweaking the internal frame resizing of the model, we explored its suitability as an accessible option for basic video analysis tasks, particularly when computational resources are limited.

It has been revealed that in our evaluation of SmolVLM's video understanding capabilities, we implemented a straightforward video processing pipeline code, extracting up to 50 evenly sampled frames from each video while avoiding internal frame resizing. This simple approach yielded surprisingly competitive results on the CinePile benchmark, with a score of 27.14%, a performance that positions the model between InternVL2 (2B) and Video LlaVa (7B).

The quantitative results align with our qualitative testing, looking at an example from the FineVideo dataset:.

While in the second question, we see some temporal understanding limitations (the cook points to one ingredient after the other rather than pointing/holding all of them at the same time) SmolVLM demonstrated great scene understanding and object recognition capabilities.

We integrated SmolVLM with VLMEvalKit to facilitate easy evaluation across additional benchmarks.

By running the following command, you can evaluate SmolVLM or your fine-tuned SmolVLM model.

For example, to evaluate on MMMU dev validation set and MathVista mini and store the results in a folder called smol.

You can easily load SmolVLM using the Auto classes in transformers. Under the hood, the model and processor are mapped to the same implementations used for Idefics3.

Image and text can be interleaved arbitrarily, and you can pass in multiple images. Here’s how you can use the chat template and pass in the formatted input to the processor.

In a recent development, first, we had to train SmolLM2 to extend it context, but we will discuss that in the next subsection. Once we had a long context SmolLM2, we trained SmolVLM using the same data that we used for Idefics3. Mainly, we used The Cauldron and Docmatix. The full list of datasets we used can be consulted here.

Sources indicate that smolLM2’s pre-training context window is insufficient for VLMs. Images are encoded into many tokens, and we wanted to support multiple images. To address this, we extended it to 16k tokens by increasing the RoPE base value from 10k to 273k, following the guidelines in “Scaling Laws of RoPE-based Extrapolation”. We fine-tuned the model on a mixture of long- and short-context datasets. For long-context datasets, we used the “books” subset of Dolma (primarily Project Gutenberg) and code documents with 8k+ tokens from The Stack, each contributing 20% to the final mixture. For short-context datasets, we streamlined the original SmolLM2 pre-training mix to include 20% FineWeb-Edu, 20% DCLM, and 20% from our math dataset (to be released soon). The math dataset was upsampled to mitigate a performance drop observed on GSM8k during the context extension process. All experiments were implemented using the EasyContext repository.

It has been revealed that for our training run, we saved checkpoints every 25 optimization steps, allowing us to evaluate and potentially recover the model's state at different points in training. This practice is crucial for identifying the optimal model version, as training longer doesn't always guarantee better performance. We evaluated the performance across multiple vision-language benchmarks, each weighted according to their importance. The core benchmarks included the following:.

To select the optimal checkpoint, we created a single metric by combining these benchmarks with different manually assigned weights to reflect their relative importance in assessing the model's capabilities. We used this single metric to select the best checkpoint. Generally, the models tended to do great on most benchmarks with more training, but their relative performance on DocVQA would decrease considerably.

You can fine-tune SmolVLM using transformers and apply alignment techniques using TRL 🚀.

It has been revealed that we provide a notebook to fine-tune it on the VQAv2 dataset, optionally using LoRA, QLoRA or full fine-tuning. In the notebook, you can find some tricks to save up even more memory and have a larger batch size to fit SmolVLM inside consumer GPUs, like L4, for training. With batch sizes of 4, 8-bit loading with QLoRA and gradient checkpointing we can fine-tune in L4, and it consumes around ~16 GBs of VRAM. This makes it possible to fine-tune your SmolVLM using Colab! You can play around with the parameters to get a nice point in training duration-memory trade-off.

SmolVLM also comes with TRL integration so you can apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) easily through the CLI. Get started by running pip install trl accelerate peft and then run the following command to fine-tune on RLAIF-V dataset:.

According to recent reports, the resulting LoRA adapter weights are SmolVLM-Instruct-DPO. A detailed tutorial on preference tuning vision-based LLM can be found here: dpo_vlm.

Tech Report: Rearchitecting Hugging Face Uploads and Downloads

📅 26 Nov 2024 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as part of Hugging Face's Xet team’s work to improve Hugging Face Hub’s storage backend, we analyzed a 24 hour window of Hugging Face upload requests to better understand access patterns.
  • The map below visualizes this activity, with countries colored by bytes uploaded per hour.
  • According to recent reports, currently, uploads are stored in an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and optimized using S3 Transfer Acceleration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as part of Hugging Face's Xet team’s work to improve Hugging Face Hub’s storage backend, we analyzed a 24 hour window of Hugging Face upload requests to better understand access patterns. On October 11th, 2024, we saw:.

The map below visualizes this activity, with countries colored by bytes uploaded per hour.

According to recent reports, currently, uploads are stored in an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and optimized using S3 Transfer Acceleration. Downloads are cached and served using AWS Cloudfront as a CDN. Cloudfront’s 400+ convenient edge locations provide global coverage and low-latency data transfers. However, like most CDNs, it is optimized for web content and has a file size limit of 50GB.

While this size restriction is reasonable for typical internet file transfers, the ever-growing size of files in model and dataset repositories presents a challenge. For instance, the weights of meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B total 131GB and are split across 30 files to meet the Hub’s recommendation of chunking weights into 20 GB segments. Additionally, to enable advanced deduplication or compression techniques for both uploads and downloads requires a reimagining of how we handle file transfers.

To push Hugging Face infrastructure beyond its current limits, we are redesigning the Hub’s upload and download architecture. We proposal to insert a content-addressed store (CAS) as the first stop for content distribution. This enables us to implement a custom protocol built on a guiding philosophy of dumb reads and smart writes. Unlike Git LFS, which treats files as opaque blobs, our approach analyzes files at the byte level, uncovering opportunities to improve transfer speeds for the massive files found in model and dataset repositories.

The read path prioritizes simplicity and speed to ensure high throughput with minimal latency. Requests for a file are routed to a CAS server, which provides reconstruction information. The data itself remains backed by an S3 bucket in us-east-1, with AWS CloudFront continuing to serve as the CDN for downloads.

The write path is more complex to optimize upload speeds and provide additional security guarantees. Like reads, upload requests are routed to a CAS server, but instead of querying at the file level we operate on chunks. As matches are found, the CAS server instructs the client (e.g., huggingface_hub) to transfer only the necessary (new) chunks. The chunks are validated by CAS before uploading them to S3.

There are many implementation details to address such as network constraints and storage overhead which we’ll cover in future posts. For now, let's look at how reads presently look. The first diagram below show the read and write path as they currently look today:.

Meanwhile, in the newly introduced design, reads will take the following path:.

and finally here is the updated write path:.

By managing files at the byte level, we can adapt optimizations to suit different file formats. For instance, we have explored improving the dedupeability of Parquet files, and are now investigating compressing tensor files (e.g., Safetensors) which have the potential to trim 10-25% off upload speeds. As upcoming formats emerge, we are uniquely positioned to develop further enhancements that improve the development experience on the Hub.

This protocol also introduces significant improvements for enterprise customers and power owners. Inserting a control plane for file transfers provides added guarantees to ensure malicious or invalid data cannot be uploaded. Operationally, uploads are no longer a black box. Enhanced telemetry provides audit trails and detailed logging, enabling the Hub infrastructure team to identify and resolve problems promptly and efficiently.

It has been revealed that to support this custom protocol, we need to determine the optimal geographic distribution for the CAS service. AWS Lambda@Edge was initially considered for its extensive global coverage to help minimize the round-trip time. However, its reliance on Cloudfront triggers made it incompatible with our updated upload path. Instead, we opted to deploy CAS nodes in a select few of AWS’s 34 regions.

Recent findings suggest that taking a closer look at our 24-hour window of S3 PUT requests, we identified global traffic patterns that reveal the distribution of data uploads to the Hub. As expected, the majority of activity comes from North America and Europe, with continuous, high-volume uploads throughout the day. The data also highlights a strong and growing presence in Asia. By focusing on these core regions, we can place our CAS points of presence to balance storage and network resources while minimizing latency.

In a recent development, while AWS offers 34 regions, our goal is to keep infrastructure costs reasonable while maintaining a high user experience. Out of the 88 countries represented in this snapshot, the Pareto chart above demonstrates that the top 7 countries account for 80% of uploaded bytes, while the top 20 countries contribute 95% of the total upload volume and requests.

The United States emerges as the primary source of upload traffic, necessitating a PoP in this region. In Europe, most activity is concentrated in central and western countries (e.g., Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, and Germany) though there is some additional activity to account for in Africa (specifically Algeria, Egypt, and South Africa). Asia’s upload traffic is primarily driven by Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, and South Korea.

If we use a simple heuristic to distribute traffic, we can divide our CAS coverage into three major regions:.

This ends up being quite effective. The US and Europe account for 78.4% of uploaded bytes, while Asia accounts for 21.6%.

This regional breakdown results in a well-balanced load across our three CAS PoPs, with additional capacity for growth in ap-southeast-1 and flexibility to scale up in us-east-1 and eu-west-3 as needed.

Based on expected traffic, we plan to allocate resources as follows:.

It has been revealed that even though we’re increasing the first hop distance for some users, the overall impact to bandwidth across the Hub will be limited. Our estimates predict that while the cumulative bandwidth for all uploads will decrease from 48.5 Mbps to 42.5 Mbps (a 12% reduction), the performance hit will be more than offset by other system optimizations.

Industry observers note that we are presently working toward moving our infrastructure into production by the end of 2024, where we will start with a single CAS in us-east-1. From there, we’ll start duplicating internal repositories to our newly introduced storage system to benchmark transfer performance, and then replicate our CAS to the additional PoPs mentioned above for more benchmarking. Based on those results, we will continue to optimize our approach to ensure that everything works smoothly when our storage backend is fully in place next year.

It has been revealed that as we continue this analysis, latest opportunities for deeper insights are emerging. Hugging Face hosts one of the largest collections of data from the open-source machine learning community, providing a unique vantage point to explore the modalities and trends driving AI development around the world.

For example, future analyses could classify models uploaded to the Hub by use case (such as NLP, computer vision, robotics, or large language models) and examine geographic trends in ML activity. This data not only informs our infrastructure decisions but also provides a lens into the evolving landscape of machine learning.

We invite you to explore our current findings in more detail! Visit our interactive Space to see the upload distribution for your region, and follow our team to hear more about what we’re building.

Industry News: Open Source Developers Guide to the EU AI Act

📅 02 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the EU AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive legislation on artificial intelligence, has officially come into force, and it’s set to impact the way we develop and use AI – including in the open source community.
  • Disclaimer: The information provided in this guide is for informational purposes only, and should not be considered as any form of legal advice.
  • According to recent reports, the EU AI Act is a binding regulation that aims to foster responsible AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the EU AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive legislation on artificial intelligence, has officially come into force, and it’s set to impact the way we develop and use AI – including in the open source community. If you’re an open source developer navigating this latest landscape, you’re probably wondering what this means for your projects. This guide breaks down key points of the regulation with a focus on open source development, offering a clear introduction to this legislation and directing you to tools that may help you prepare to comply with it.

Disclaimer: The information provided in this guide is for informational purposes only, and should not be considered as any form of legal advice.

According to recent reports, the EU AI Act is a binding regulation that aims to foster responsible AI. To that end, it sets out rules that scale with the level of risk the AI system or model might pose while aiming to preserve open research and support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). As an open source developer, many aspects of your work won’t be directly impacted – especially if you’re already documenting your systems and keeping track of data sources. In general, there are straightforward steps you can take to prepare for compliance.

Recent findings suggest that the regulation takes effect over the next two years and applies broadly, not just to those within the EU. If you’re an open source developer outside the EU but your AI systems or models are offered or impact people within the EU, they are included in the Act.

The regulation works at different levels of the AI stack, meaning it has different obligations if you are a provider (which includes the developers), deployer, distributor etc. and if you are working on an AI model or system.

In the AI Act, rules scale with the level of risk the AI system or model might pose. For all AI systems, risks may be:.

For general purpose AI (GPAI) models, there is another risk category called systemic risk: GPAI models using substantial computing power, today defined as over 10^25 FLOPs for training, or that have high-impact capabilities. According to a study by Stanford, in August 2024, based on estimates from Epoch, only eight models (Gemini 1.0 Ultra, Llama 3.1-405B, GPT-4, Mistral Large, Nemotron-4 340B, MegaScale, Inflection-2, Inflection-2.5) from seven developers (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Mistral, NVIDIA, ByteDance, Inflection) would meet the default systemic risk criterion of being trained using at least 10^25 FLOPs. Obligations vary if they are open source or not.

Sources indicate that our focus in this short guide is on limited risk AI systems and open source non-systemic risk GPAI models, which should encompass most of what is publicly available on the Hub. For other risk categories, make sure to check out further obligations that may apply.

Sources indicate that limited-risk AI systems interact directly with people (end owners) and may create risks of impersonation, manipulation, or deception. For example, a chatbot producing text or a text-to-image generator – tools that can also facilitate the creation of misinformation materials or of deepfakes. The AI Act aims to tackle these risks by helping the general end user understand that they are interacting with an AI system. Today, most GPAI models are not considered to present systemic risk. In the case of limited-risk AI systems, the obligations below apply whether or not they are open source.

Developers of limited-risk AI systems need to:.

Recent findings suggest that note that you may also be a ‘deployer’ of an AI system, not only a developer. Deployers of AI systems are people or companies using an AI system in their professional capacity. In that case, you also need to comply with the following:.

The information above needs to be provided with clear language, at the latest at the time of the user’s first interaction with, or exposure, to the AI system.

The AI Office, in charge of implementing the AI Act, will help create codes of practice with guidelines for detecting and labeling artificially generated content. These codes are currently being written with industry and civil society participation, and are expected to be published by May 2025. Obligations will be enforced starting August 2026.

Sources indicate that the following obligations apply if you are developing open source GPAI models, e.g. LLMs, that do not present systemic risk. Open source for the AI Act means “software and data, including models, released under a free and open source license that allows them to be openly shared and where customers can freely access, use, modify and redistribute them or modified versions thereof”. Developers can select from a list of open licenses on the Hub. Check if the chosen license fits the AI Act’s open source definition.

The obligations for non-systemic open source GPAI models are as follows:.

Developers may rely on codes of practice (which are currently being developed and expected by May 2025) to demonstrate compliance with these obligations.

Other obligations apply if you make your work available in a way that does not meet the criteria for being open source according to the AI Act.

Also, note that if a given GPAI model meets the conditions to pose systemic risks, its developers must notify the EU Commission. In the notification process, developers can argue that their model does not present systemic risks because of specific characteristics. The Commission will review each argument and accept or reject the claim depending on whether the argument is sufficiently substantiated, considering the model’s specific characteristics and capabilities. If the Commission rejects the developers’ arguments, the GPAI model will be designated as posing systemic risk and will need to comply with further obligations, such as providing technical documentation on the model including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation.

Obligations for GPAI models will be enforced starting August 2025.

Much of the EU AI Act’s practical application is still in development through public consultations and working groups, whose outcome will determine how the Act’s provisions aimed at smoother compliance for SMEs and researchers are operationalized. If you’re interested in shaping how this plays out, now is a great time to get involved!

Thank you, Anna Tordjmann, Brigitte Tousignant, Chun Te Lee, Irene Solaiman, Clémentine Fourrier, Ann Huang, Benjamin Burtenshaw, Florent Daudens for your feedback, comments, and suggestions.

Investing in Performance: Fine-tune small models with LLM insights - a CFM case study

📅 03 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Overview: This article presents a deep dive into Capital Fund Management’s (CFM) use of open-source large language models (LLMs) and the Hugging Face (HF) ecosystem to optimize Named Entity Recognition (NER) for financial data.
  • This structured approach combines accuracy and cost-effectiveness, making it ideal for real-world financial applications.
  • Capital Fund Management (CFM) is an alternative investment management firm headquartered in Paris, also has teams in New York City and London right now overseeing assets totaling 15.5 billion dollars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Overview: This article presents a deep dive into Capital Fund Management’s (CFM) use of open-source large language models (LLMs) and the Hugging Face (HF) ecosystem to optimize Named Entity Recognition (NER) for financial data. By leveraging LLM-assisted labeling with HF Inference Endpoints and refining data with Argilla, the team improved accuracy by up to 6.4% and reduced operational costs, achieving solutions up to 80x cheaper than large LLMs alone.

This structured approach combines accuracy and cost-effectiveness, making it ideal for real-world financial applications.

Capital Fund Management (CFM) is an alternative investment management firm headquartered in Paris, also has teams in New York City and London right now overseeing assets totaling 15.5 billion dollars.

Employing a scientific approach to finance, CFM leverages quantitative and systematic methods to devise superior investment strategies.

Recent findings suggest that CFM has been working with Hugging Face's Expert Support to stay updated on the latest advancements in machine learning and harness the power of open-source technology for their wide range of financial applications. One of the collaboration's main goals has been to explore how CFM can benefit from efficiently using open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance their existing machine learning use cases. Quantitative hedge funds rely on massive amounts of data to inform decisions about whether to buy or sell specific financial products. In addition to standard data sources from financial markets (e.g., prices), hedge funds are increasingly extracting insights from alternative data, such as textual information from news articles. One major challenge in incorporating news into fully automated trading strategies is accurately identifying the products or entities (e.g., companies, stocks, currencies) mentioned in the articles. While CFM’s data providers supply these tags, they can be incomplete and require further validation.

In a recent development, CFM explored several approaches to improve financial entity recognition, including zero-shot NER using LLMs and smaller models, LLM-assisted data labeling with Hugging Face Inference Endpoints and Argilla, and fine-tuning smaller models on curated datasets. These approaches not only leverage the versatility of large models but also address the challenges of cost and scalability in real-world financial applications.

Among open-source models, the Llama 3.1 series by Meta stood out due to its strong performance across benchmarks, making it a top choice for generating synthetic annotations. These LLMs were pivotal in creating high-quality labeled datasets, combining automation and human expertise to streamline the labeling process and enhance model performance in financial NER tasks.

In a recent development, our focus on this use case was to extract company names from news headlines from the Financial News and Stock Price Integration Dataset (FNSPID). It is composed of news headlines and articles associated with corresponding stock symbols coming from several sources such as Bloomberg, Reuters, Benzinga and others. After analyzing the various news sources, we found that news from Benzinga had no missing stock symbol values. This subset of the dataset contains ~900k samples. As a result, we decided to reduce our dataset to Benzinga headlines for a more consistent and reliable analysis.

Example samples and target predictions for the task.

To effectively compare different approaches, we first need to consolidate a reliable dataset that will serve as a foundation for evaluating the candidate methods. This dataset will be used for both testing the performance of models in zero-shot settings and as a base for fine-tuning.

We used Llama-assisted data labeling to streamline and enhance the annotation process by having Llama 3.1 generate labels for dataset samples. These auto-generated labels were then manually reviewed using the open-source data annotation platform Argilla. This approach allowed us to speed up the labeling process while ensuring the quality of the annotations.

To securely and swiftly get access to a Llama3.1-70-Instruct deployment we opted for Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

In a recent development, hugging Face Inference Endpoints provide a straightforward and secure solution for deploying machine learning models in production environments. They enable developers and data scientists to build AI applications without the need to manage infrastructure, simplifying deployment to just a few clicks.

To access Inference Endpoints we logged in as a member of the CapitalFundManagement organization on the Hugging Face Hub, then accessed the service at https://ui.endpoints.huggingface.co . To start a new deployment we create on New then select meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct.

Endpoint creation on the Inference Endpoints UI.

You can select on which cloud provider the hardware will be hosted,  the region, and the type of instance. Inference Endpoints suggest an instance type based on the model size, which should be big enough to run the model. Here an instance with 4 Nvidia L40S is selected. When LLM is selected, an automated container is selected running Text Generation Inference for optimized inference.

According to recent reports, when clicking on the “Create Endpoint” the deployment is created and the endpoint will be ready in a few minutes. To get more information about Inference Endpoints setup, visit https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-endpoints.

Endpoint running on the Inference Endpoints UI.

Once our endpoint is running, we will use the endpoint URL provided to send requests to it.

Industry observers note that before sending requests, we needed to design a prompt that would guide the model effectively to generate the desired output. After several rounds of testing, we structured the prompt into multiple sections to address the task accurately:.

Role Definition: The model is positioned as a financial expert with strong English skills.

Task Instructions: The model is instructed to extract manufacturer names linked to stocks mentioned in headlines, while excluding stock indices often found in titles.

Expected Output: The model must return a dictionary with:.

Sources indicate that few-shot Examples: A series of input-output examples to demonstrate the expected behavior and ensure consistency in performance across varied inputs. These examples help the model understand how to distinguish relevant entities and format its output correctly. Each example illustrates different headline structures to prepare the model for a range of real-world cases.

Sources indicate that now that we have our prompt and endpoint ready, the next step is to send requests using the titles from our dataset. To do this efficiently, we'll use the AsyncInferenceClient from the huggingface_hub library. This is an asynchronous version of the InferenceClient, built on asyncio and aiohttp. It allows us to send multiple concurrent requests to the endpoint, making the processing of the dataset faster and more efficient.

To make sure the model replies a structured output, we will use guidance with a specific Pydantic schema Companies.

We also set generation parameters:.

Now we define our functions to send requests to the endpoint and parse output:.

We test the endpoint with a single example:.

According to recent reports, now, we create a process_batch function to handle sending requests in manageable batches, preventing the API endpoint from becoming overwhelmed or hitting rate limits. This batching approach allows us to efficiently process multiple requests concurrently without saturating the server, reducing the risk of timeouts, rejected requests, or throttling. By controlling the flow of requests, we ensure stable performance, faster response times, and easier error handling while maximizing throughput.

We will run inference over the dataset:.

And we create the main inference loop:.

When the inference is running we can monitor the traffic directly from the UI.

It took about 8 hours to process the whole dataset with 900k samples which costs  ~$70.

In a recent development, with the labeled data generated from our LLM, the next step is to curate a high-quality subset to ensure reliable evaluation of different methods, including zero-shot and fine-tuning approaches. This carefully reviewed dataset will also serve as a foundational base for fine-tuning smaller models. The entire labeled dataset by the LLM can be also used for fine-tuning in a weak supervision framework.

Industry observers note that to create a manageable sample size for review, we used LLM labels and clustered company names using fuzzy matching with the rapidfuzz library. We applied the cdist function to compute Levenshtein distances between companies and clustered them with a threshold of 85. A representative company was selected for each cluster, and Llama predictions were mapped accordingly. Finally, we sampled 5% of news headlines from each company-related cluster and 5% from headlines without any companies resulting in a dataset of 2714 samples. Then using metadata, the sampled dataset is divided into three parts:.

Train: News from 2010 to 2016, used for training small ML models - 2405 samples.

Validation: News from 2017 to 2018, for hyperparameters tuning - 204 samples.

Test: News from 2019 to 2020, used to evaluate the model on unseen data. - 105 samples.

Once created, we set up an annotation tool, Argilla, to ease the annotation process.

It has been revealed that argilla is an open-source tool, integrated into the Hugging Face ecosystem that excels at gathering human feedback for a wide range of AI projects. Whether you're working on traditional NLP tasks like text classification and NER, fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or preference tuning, or developing multimodal models like text-to-image systems, Argilla provides the tools needed to collect and refine feedback efficiently. This ensures your models continuously improve based on high-quality, human-validated data.An Argilla interface can be set up directly through Hugging Face Spaces and this is what we opted for. Check out the documentation to start your own interface and go to https://huggingface.co/newly introduced-space .

Create Argilla Space on the Hub.

It has been revealed that once the interface is created, we can connect programmatically to it using the Argilla python SDK. To get ready to annotate we followed the following steps:.

Industry observers note that the annotation interface displays the text to be annotated, along with its status (either pending or submitted). Annotation guidelines are presented on the right side of the screen. In this case, we have one label, 'Organization.' To annotate, we first select the label, then highlight the relevant text in the sentence. Once all entities are selected, we click 'submit' to finalize the annotation.

Recent findings suggest that using pre-computed Llama labels significantly accelerates the annotation process, reducing the time per sample to just 5 to 10 seconds, compared to roughly 30 seconds for raw, unprocessed samples. This efficiency leads to a substantial time saving, allowing us to complete the annotation of 2,714 samples in around 8 hours. The efficiency gains are even more pronounced for more complex tasks than NER, where the time saved with pre-computed labels or generation becomes significantly greater.

Sources indicate that with a high-quality, reviewed dataset in place, we can now experiment with different approaches for zero-shot NER. We tested four models:.

GLiNER is a compact, versatile NER model that leverages bidirectional transformers like BERT to identify a wide range of entity types overcoming the limitations of traditional models that are restricted to predefined entities. Unlike large autoregressive models, GLiNER treats NER as a task of matching entity types with spans in text, using parallel processing for efficiency. It offers a practical and resource-efficient alternative to LLMs, delivering strong performance in zero-shot scenarios without the high computational costs associated with larger models.

GLiNER architecture from the original paper<.

GLiNER offers three model variants:.

According to recent reports, compared to LLMs like Llama-3.1-70b, GLiNER models are more compact, cost-effective, and efficient for NER tasks, while LLMs generally offer broader flexibility but are much larger and resource-intensive. GLiNER medium can be tried on the Hugging Face Space: https://huggingface.co/spaces/tomaarsen/gliner_medium-v2.1 For our experiments, we focused our attention on a specific GLiNER variant EmergentMethods/gliner_medium_news-v2.1 which has been already fine-tuned on the EmergentMethods/AskNews-NER-v0 and aims at improving the accuracy across a wide range of topic and especially for long-context news entity recognition extraction.To use GLiNER you can install the gliner package based out of the Hugging Face transformers library.

Then using GLiNER for NER is as easy as:.

For a list of samples the batch_text method can be used:.

The zero-shot results, in terms of F1-score on the annotated dataset of 2714 samples curated earlier is 87%.

In a recent development, the GLiNER model performs well in extracting tech giant names from text but struggles with certain cases, such as when companies are mentioned as stock symbols. It also misclassifies general references to stock industries, like "Healthcare stocks" or "Industrial stocks," as company names. While effective in many cases, these errors highlight areas where further refinement is needed to improve accuracy in distinguishing between companies and broader industry terms.

It has been revealed that the zero-shot results, in terms of F1-score on the annotated dataset of 2714 samples curated earlier is 47%. SpanMarker model performs well in extracting accurate company names but tends to identify too many incorrect entities. This is due to its training on the broader "organization" category, which includes entities such as non-profit organizations, government bodies, educational institutions, and sports teams. As a result, it sometimes confuses these with company names, leading to over-extraction and less precise results in certain contexts.

We tested 2 variants of the Llama3.1 model including the 70b that we used to curate ground truth examples. We used the prompt that is presented above. On our annotated subset we have the following results :.

It has been revealed that in this experiment, we compared the performance of small models like GLiNER and SpanMarker against LLMs such as Llama 3.1-8b and Llama 3.1-70b. Small models like GLiNER (87% F1) provide a good balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, making them ideal for resource-constrained scenarios. In contrast, LLMs, while more resource-intensive, deliver higher accuracy, with Llama 3.1-70b achieving a 95% F1-score. This highlights the trade-off between performance and efficiency when choosing between small models and LLMs for NER tasks. Let’s now see how the performance differs when we fine-tune compact models.

According to recent reports, using our train/validation/test subsets created earlier, we fine-tuned GLiNER and SpanMarker on an AWS instance with a single Nvidia A10 GPU. A fine-tuning example for GLiNER is accessible here and for SpanMarker here. Fine-tuning those models is as easy as running this with train_datasetand valid_datasetcreated as Hugging Face dataset.

The training ran for 20 epochs, we save the checkpoint with the highest F1 score on the validation set.

In this updated comparison, we evaluated models based on their F1-scores after fine-tuning. The GLiNER-medium-news model improved from 87.0% to 93.4% after fine-tuning, showing significant gains in accuracy. Similarly, SpanMarker went from 47.0% to 90.1% with fine-tuning, making it far more competitive. Meanwhile, Llama 3.1-8b and Llama 3.1-70b performed well out of the box, scoring 80.0% and 92.7%, respectively, without fine-tuning. This comparison emphasizes that fine-tuning smaller models like GLiNER and SpanMarker can dramatically enhance performance, rivaling larger LLMs at a lower computational cost.

The llama 3.1-70b model costs at least $8 per hour for inference, making it significantly more expensive than compact models, which can run on a GPU instance costing around $0.50 per hour—16 times cheaper. Furthermore, compact models can even be deployed on CPU instances, costing as little as ~$0.10 per hour, which is 80 times less expensive. This highlights the substantial cost advantage of smaller models, especially in resource-constrained environments, without sacrificing competitive performance when fine-tuned for specific tasks.

In this experiment, we explored two key approaches to data labeling for NER: Weak Supervision and LLM-assisted labeling. While weak supervision enables scalable training on synthetic data, our findings suggest that it cannot achieve the same level of accuracy as models trained on manually annotated data. For 1,000 samples, manual annotation took 3 hours with an F1 score of 0.915, while Llama 3.1-70b inference only took 2 minutes but resulted in a slightly lower F1 score of 0.895. The trade-off between speed and accuracy depends on the task's requirements.

Weak Supervision vs. LLM-assisted labeling.

The graph compares the performance of GLiNER fine-tuned on human-annotated data versus synthetic data inferred by Llama-3.1 70b across varying dataset sizes. The blue dots represent F1-scores of models trained on human-annotated data, while the red dots represent those inferred by Llama-3.1 70b. As dataset size increases, models fine-tuned on human annotations consistently outperform those using synthetic data, achieving higher F1-scores. It illustrates that while models fine-tuned on human annotations yield higher accuracy,_ LLM-assisted labeling using Llama-3.1 70b can still provide considerable value, especially when resources for manual annotation are limited. Even though the F1-scores from LLM-inferred data are slightly lower, they remain competitive across various dataset sizes. LLMs can rapidly generate large volumes of annotations, offering a practical solution for scaling dataset creation efficiently, making them beneficial in scenarios where time and cost constraints are critical.

According to recent reports, our experiment demonstrated that while large models like Llama 3.1 provide superior performance out of the box, fine-tuning smaller models like GLiNER and SpanMarker with LLM-assisted labeling can significantly enhance accuracy, rivaling the LLMs at a fraction of the cost. This approach highlights how investing in fine-tuning small models using LLM insights provides a cost-effective, scalable solution for financial NER tasks, making it ideal for real-world applications where both accuracy and resource efficiency are crucial.

For a wider field, see our guide to the best AI recruiting agents.

Noon details come from Noon's own pages or a named third party, checked October 14, 2026.

Sources indicate that pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that assists recruiters by finding candidates across the 850M+ profiles Pin states it covers across North America and Europe, writing outreach from each person's profile signals and booking interviews. Candidate data comes from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. You search in plain language, paste a job description, upload ideal résumés or import a role from your ATS. Each ranked candidate has a fit score and an AI-written reason, and the model learns from your team's accept and reject feedback.

The Pin recruiting agent has two modes. In Assist you approve each step. In Autopilot it sources, screens and ranks, drafts outreach, sends the email steps, follows up on silence, schedules interviews and updates your ATS. LinkedIn and SMS steps arrive as tasks with an AI-drafted message, and you send them. Closing and offers stay human. The agent asks clarifying questions ("Is remote considered?"), shows every action in a feed and works 24/7 alongside your team. Josh Volinsky, Co-Founder of Synergy Search, indicates: "Pin makes sourcing candidates so natural and I love how you can just talk to it like it's a recruiter on your team and it goes hunting.".

Noon (noon.ai) is an AI recruiting platform from Portal Inc. in New York whose agents source across the open web, run email and SMS outreach and book interviews. You start from a pasted job description or posting URL. Noon extracts the title, location and "non-negotiables," and its Autopilot sourcing agent keeps searching as new people enter the market. Candidates land in a ranked feed with reasoning, and thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback calibrates the search per role.

According to recent reports, noon also extends further down the funnel. Its AI Interviewer runs voice screening calls, its Notetaker joins live interviews, and Inbound Screening ranks ATS applicants and flags suspected fraud. Those tools sit downstream of sourcing. Pin concentrates on the outbound workflow, from search through scheduling, and adds the team layer around it: a shared inbox, a dedupe layer so two recruiters never contact the same person, funnel dashboards and a multi-client CRM for agencies.

Pin gives you natural-language filters plus advanced filters you set yourself, and paid intends include unlimited searches.

According to recent reports, noon steers the search through criteria set per role. Its pages describe titles, locations, years of experience, target-manufacturer lists and must-haves, plus non-negotiables Noon says it never relaxes. You adjust by chat and feedback. We found no public description of an open-ended filter panel like Pin's, so ask for one in a demo if ad hoc searching matters.

Sources indicate that on consistency, Pin returns a ranked shortlist with a reason for every candidate from the first search, then improves as your team accepts and rejects. Noon says its feedback loop calibrates the model per role, but it doesn't say how long that takes. Compare day one with day ten yourself (see the trial strategy below).

Recent findings suggest that pin writes each message from the candidate's profile signals and calibrates to your writing voice.
