Loading these datasets is rather simple, e.g.:.

The gooaq dataset doesn't already have a train-eval split, so we can make one with train_test_split. Otherwise, we can just load a precomputed split with e.g. split="eval".

It has been revealed that note that train_test_split does mean that the dataset has to be loaded into memory, whereas it is otherwise just kept on disk. This increased memory is not ideal when training, so it's recommended to 1) load the data, 2) split it, and 3) save it to disk with save_to_disk. Before training, you can then use load_from_disk to load it again.

Industry observers note that within Sentence Transformers, your loss model must match your training data format. The Loss Overview is designed as an overview of which losses are compatible with which formats.

In particular, we at the moment have the following formats in our data:.

For these formats, we have some excellent choices:.

It has been revealed that multipleNegativesRankingLoss (MNRL): Also known as in-batch negatives loss or InfoNCE loss, this loss has been used to train modern embedding models for a handful of years. In short, the loss optimizes the following:.

Given an anchor (e.g. a question), assign the highest similarity to the corresponding positive (i.e. answer) out of all positives and negatives (e.g. all answers) in the batch.

If you provide the optional negatives, they will only be used as extra options (also known as in-batch negatives) from which the model must pick the correct positive. Within reason, the harder this "picking" is, the stronger the model will become. Because of this, higher batch sizes result in more in-batch negatives, which then increase performance (to a point).

CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss (CMNRL): This is an extension of MNRL that implements GradCache, an approach that allows for arbitrarily increasing the batch size without increasing the memory.

This loss is recommended over MNRL unless you can already fit a large enough batch size in memory with just MNRL. In that case, you can use MNRL to save the 20% training speed cost that CMNRL adds.

GISTEmbedLoss (GIST): This is also an extension of MNRL, it uses a guide Sentence Transformer model to remove potential false negatives from the list of options that the model must "pick" the correct positive from.

False negatives can hurt performance, but hard true negatives (texts that are close to correct, but not quite) can help performance, so this filtering is a fine line to walk.

Because these static embedding models are extremely small, it is possible to fit our desired batch size of 2048 samples on our hardware: a single RTX 3090 with 24GB, so we don't need to use CMNRL.

In a recent development, additionally, because we're training such fast models, the guide from the GISTEmbedLoss would make the training much slower. Because of this, we've opted to use MultipleNegativesRankingLoss for our models.

Industry observers note that if we were to try these experiments again, we would pick a larger batch size, e.g. 16384 with CMNRL. If you try, please let us know how it goes!

It has been revealed that beyond regular loss functions, Sentence Transformers also implements a handful of Loss modifiers. These work on top of standard loss functions, but apply them in different ways to try and instil useful properties into the trained embedding model.

Sources indicate that A very interesting one is the MatryoshkaLoss, which turns the trained model into a Matryoshka Model. This allows people to truncate the output embeddings at a minimal loss of performance, meaning that retrieval or clustering can be sped up due to the smaller dimensionalities.

The MatryoshkaLoss is applied on top of a normal loss. It's recommended to also include the normal embedding dimensionality in the list of matryoshka_dims:.

Sentence Transformers supports a lot of training arguments, the most valuable of which have been listed in the Training Overview > Training Arguments documentation.

We used the same core training parameters to train both models:.

Beyond these core arguments, we also set a few training arguments for tracking and debugging: eval_strategy, eval_steps, save_strategy, save_steps, save_total_limit, logging_steps, logging_first_step, and run_name.

In the end, we used these SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments for the two models:.

Industry observers note that if we provide an evaluation dataset to the Sentence Transformer Trainer, then upon evaluation we will get an evaluation loss. This'll be useful to track whether we're overfitting or not, but not so meaningful when it comes to real downstream performance.

Because of this, Sentence Transformers additionally supports Evaluators. Unlike the training loss, these give qualitative metrics like NDCG, MAP, MRR for Information Retrieval, Spearman Correlation for Semantic Textual Similarity, or Triplet accuracy (number of samples where similarity(anchor, positive) > similarity(anchor, negative)).

Due to its simplicity, we will be using the NanoBEIREvaluator for the retrieval model. This evaluator runs Information Retrieval benchmarks on the NanoBEIR collection of datasets. This dataset is a subset of the much larger (and thus slower) BEIR benchmark, which is commonly used as the Retrieval tab in the MTEB Leaderboard.

Because all datasets are already pre-defined, we can load the evaluator without any arguments:.

We're training these models on consumer-level hardware, specifically:.

This section contains the final training scripts for both models with all of the previously described components (datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluator, trainer) combined.

This script produced sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 after 17.8 hours of training. In total, it consumed 2.6 kWh of energy and emitted 1kg of CO2. That is roughly equivalent to the amount of CO2 an average person exhales per day.

See our Weights and Biases report for the training and evaluation metrics collected during training.

This script produced sentence-transformers/static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 after 3.1 hours of training. In total, it consumed 0.5 kWh of energy and emitted 0.2kg of CO2. That is roughly 20% of the CO2 that an average person exhales per day.

See our Weights and Biases report for the training and evaluation losses collected during training.

The usage of these models is very straightforward, identical to the normal Sentence Transformers flow:.

The upcoming Performance > English Retrieval section will show that these results are quite solid, within 15% of commonly used Transformer-based encoder models like all-mpnet-base-v2.

This model only loses about 8% of performance compared to the popular but much slower multilingual-e5-small, as shown in the upcoming Performance > Multilingual Similarity section.

To reduce the dimensionality of your calculated embeddings, you can simply pass the truncate_dim parameter. This works for all Sentence Transformer models.

This model also works out of the box in various third party libraries, for example LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai.

After training, we've evaluated the final model sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 on NanoBEIR (normal dimensionality and with Matryoshka dimensions) as well as on BEIR.

According to recent reports, we've evaluated sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 on NanoBEIR and plotted it against the inference speed computed on our hardware. For the inference speed tests, we calculated the number of computed query embeddings of the GooAQ dataset per second, either on CPU or GPU.

We evaluate against 3 types of models:.

Attention-based dense embedding models, e.g. traditional Sentence Transformer models like all-mpnet-base-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5, and gte-large-en-v1.5.

Sources indicate that static Embedding-based models, e.g. static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1, potion-base-8M, M2V_base_output, and glove.6B.300d.

Sparse bag-of-words model, BM25, often a strong baseline.

We relied on the highly efficient bm25s implementation, using model.get_scores() on tokens after tokenization and stemming with the English PyStemmer.

NOTE: Many of the attention-based dense embedding models are finetuned on the training splits of the (Nano)BEIR evaluation datasets. This gives the models an unfair advantage in this benchmark and can result in lower downstream performance on real retrieval tasks.

static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 is purposefully not trained on any of these datasets.

We can draw some notable conclusions from these figures:.

Additionally, we experimented with the results on NanoBEIR performance when we performed Matryoshka-style dimensionality reduction by truncating the output embeddings to a lower dimensionality.

These findings show that reducing the dimensionality by e.g. 2x only has a 1.47% reduction in performance (0.5031 NDCG@10 vs 0.4957 NDCG@10), while realistically resulting in a 2x speedup in retrieval speed.

We've additionally evaluated the final sentence-transformers/static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 model on 5 languages which have a lot of benchmarks across various tasks on MTEB.

We want to reiterate that this model is not intended for retrieval use cases. Instead, we evaluate on Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), Classification, and Pair Classification. We compare against the excellent and small multilingual-e5-small model.

Across all measured languages, static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 reaches an average 92.3% for STS, 95.52% for Pair Classification, and 86.52% for Classification relative to multilingual-e5-small.

To make up for this performance reduction, static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 is approximately ~125x faster on CPU and ~10x faster on GPU devices than multilingual-e5-small. Due to the super-linear nature of attention models, versus the linear nature of static embedding models, the speedup will only grow larger as the number of tokens to encode increases.

Lastly, we experimented with the impacts on English STS on MTEB performance when we did Matryoshka-style dimensionality reduction by truncating the output embeddings to a lower dimensionality.

Sources indicate that as you can see, you can easily reduce the dimensionality by 2x or 4x with minor (0.15% or 0.56%) performance hits. If the speed of your downstream task or your storage costs are a bottleneck, this should allow you to alleviate some of those concerns.

This blogpost described all of the steps that we undertook from ideation to finished models, in addition to details regarding usage and evaluation of the two resulting models: static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 and static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1.

Should you need an efficient CPU-only dense embedding model for your retrieval or similarity tasks, then static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 and static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 will be extremely performant solutions at minimal costs that get surprisingly close to the attention-based dense models.

Recent findings suggest that try it out! If you already use a Sentence Transformer model somewhere, feel free to swap it out for static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 or static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1. Or, better yet: train your own models on data that is representative for the task and language of your interest.

Furthermore, some questions remain about the trained models:.

It has been revealed that because Static Embedding-based models aren't bottlenecked by positional embeddings or superlinear time complexity, they can have arbitrarily high maximum sequence lengths. However, at some point the law of large numbers is likely to "normalize" all embeddings for really long documents, such that they aren't useful anymore.

It has been revealed that more experiments are required to determine what a good cutoff point is. For now, we leave the maximum sequence length, chunking, etc. to the user.

In a recent development, additionally, there are quite a few possible extensions that are likely to improve the performance of this model, which we happily leave to other model authors. We are also open to collaborations:.

It has been revealed that may you clarifyfromhttps://huggingface.co/blog/Pringled/model2vecZipfAs we take a simple mean over tokens in the space, it is important that the vectors are weighted correctly. Normally, a sentence transformer would be there to correctly weight all the tokens for us given the context, but we don't have that luxury any more. Intuitively, we would like to use something like Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) to down-weight very frequent or uninteresting words. But we don't have access to a corpus over which to compute document frequencies.

Recent findings suggest that to overcome this, we opt to use a well-known principle from language sciences, which is that, given a frequency ranked list, the frequency of the items in that list follow a power law distribution. This is called Zipf's law. So, if we take the assumption that a vocabulary is ranked by frequency, we can accurately down-weight really frequent items without needing to have access to actual frequencies. As tokenizer vocabularies are sorted by frequency, we already have access to a ranked list, so this optimization can be applied without any additional work.

[ [0.4, 0.3, 0.2]/n1 , [ 0.2,0.5,0.7]/n2 , [1.2, 0.9,0.2] /n3 ,[1.3, 2.4, 3.2]/n4 ].

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that since its initial release in 2022, Text-Generation-Inference (TGI) has provided Hugging Face and the AI Community with a performance-focused solution to easily deploy large-language models (LLMs).
  • To address this, we are excited to introduce the concept of TGI Backends.
  • The Hugging Face team is excited to contribute to and collaborate with the teams that build vLLM, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, and the teams at AWS, Google, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel to offer a robust and consistent user experience for TGI owners whichever backend and hardware they want to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that since its initial release in 2022, Text-Generation-Inference (TGI) has provided Hugging Face and the AI Community with a performance-focused solution to easily deploy large-language models (LLMs). TGI initially offered an almost no-code solution to load models from the Hugging Face Hub and deploy them in production on NVIDIA GPUs. Over time, support expanded to include AMD Instinct GPUs, Intel GPUs, AWS Trainium/Inferentia, Google TPU, and Intel Gaudi.Over the years, multiple inferencing solutions have emerged, including vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, etc., splitting up the overall ecosystem. Different models, hardware, and use cases may require a specific backend to achieve optimal performance. However, configuring each backend correctly, managing licenses, and integrating them into existing infrastructure can be challenging for owners.

To address this, we are excited to introduce the concept of TGI Backends. This fresh architecture gives the flexibility to integrate with any of the solutions above through TGI as a single unified frontend layer. This change makes it easier for the community to get the best performance for their production workloads, switching backends according to their modeling, hardware, and performance requirements.

The Hugging Face team is excited to contribute to and collaborate with the teams that build vLLM, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, and the teams at AWS, Google, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel to offer a robust and consistent user experience for TGI owners whichever backend and hardware they want to use.

TGI is made of multiple components, primarily written in Rust and Python. Rust powers the HTTP and scheduling layers, and Python remains the go-to for modeling.

Long story short: Rust allows us to improve the overall robustness of the serving layer with static analysis and compiler-based memory safety enforcement: it brings the ability to scale to multiple cores with the same safety guarantees more easily. Leveraging Rust’s strong type system for the HTTP layer and scheduler makes it possible to avoid memory issues while maximizing the concurrency, bypassing Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in Python-based environments.

Speaking about Rust… Surprise, that's the TGI starting point to integrate a upcoming backend - 🤗.

Earlier this year, the TGI team worked on exposing the foundational knobs to disentangle how the actual HTTP server and the scheduler were coupled together. This work introduced the newly introduced Rust trait Backend to interface current inference engine and the one to come.

Having this new Backend interface (or trait in Rusty terms) paves the way for modularity and makes it possible to actually route the incoming requests towards different modeling and execution engines.

According to recent reports, the fresh multi-backend capabilities of TGI open up many impactful roadmap opportunities. As we look ahead to 2025 we are excited to share some of the TGI developments we are most excited about:.

In a recent development, we are confident TGI Backends will help simplify the deployments of LLMs, bringing versatility and performance to all TGI people. You'll soon be able to use TGI Backends directly within Inference Endpoints. Customers will be able to easily deploy models with TGI Backends on various hardware with top-tier performance and reliability out of the box.

Stay tuned for the next blog post where we'll dig into technical details and performance benchmarks of upcoming backends!

Recent findings suggest that you no longer need to build a dashboard every time you want to investigate a drop in traffic or compare campaign results. With servers built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), you can ask an AI assistant a question and let it retrieve the relevant data directly from your marketing tools.

But connecting an assistant to Google Analytics is not the same as connecting it to HubSpot or Ahrefs. Each server exposes different data, capabilities and levels of access. Some are built for quick analysis inside one platform, while others support reporting across several channels. This guide compares four servers, what they can do, how they are set up and where their limits matter. Details such as plans and tool lists change often, so confirm them against each vendor's documentation before you commit.

The summary below reflects each vendor's documentation at the time of writing.

According to recent reports, google publishes an official, open-source Google Analytics MCP server for GA4. It connects AI assistants to the Admin and Data APIs, so it can list accounts and properties, run standard, realtime, funnel and conversion reports, and inspect custom dimensions and metrics. That makes it useful for investigating traffic changes, landing page performance and engagement trends.

Example prompt: "Which landing pages lost the most engaged sessions this month compared with last month?" The assistant can pull the relevant reports and help you spot changes, and you can then check whether the decline comes from specific channels, countries or devices.

It has been revealed that setup: The server runs locally. Google's documentation lists Python 3.10 or later, pipx or uvx, a Google Cloud project with the Analytics Admin and Data APIs enabled, application default credentials with the read-only Analytics scope, and at least Viewer access on the property you want to query.

Access: Google describes the server as available for read requests only, so it cannot change your Analytics configuration.

Limitations: It covers GA4 only, so it cannot combine website metrics with CRM records or advertising costs on its own. Running it locally also means you maintain the configuration yourself.

Best for: Web analysts and technical marketers who regularly investigate GA4 performance.

Marketing performance usually spans several platforms. Google Ads generates clicks, GA4 tracks site activity and a CRM records leads. Seeing the whole picture means bringing those metrics together.

Coupler is a no-code data integration platform that offers MCP access to prepared business data. It lists more than 400 supported data sources, including Google Ads, Facebook Ads, GA4, HubSpot, LinkedIn Ads and Shopify, and lets teams combine and transform data before an assistant queries it.

Example prompt: "What was our cost per lead across Google Ads, Meta Ads and LinkedIn last quarter?" For paid search specifically, Coulper describes a Google Ads MCP server that lets you ask about campaigns and compare them with other connected channels.

Setup: Coupler is hosted, so there is nothing to install locally. You connect your platforms, configure data flows, choose refresh schedules and connect a compatible AI assistant. According to the vendor, queries run against the prepared datasets, which is useful for recurring reports because teams can reuse refreshed data instead of preparing exports by hand.

It has been revealed that limitations: Answers depend on the data included in your configured flows. Plan requirements and privacy options can vary by subscription, so check the current plan details before you rely on it.

Best for: Agencies and teams that need consistent reporting across advertising, website analytics, ecommerce and CRM platforms.

HubSpot's remote MCP server became generally available on April 13, 2026. It connects compatible AI clients to CRM data such as contacts, companies, deals, tickets and activities, and can also read marketing objects such as campaigns, landing pages and blog posts. That helps marketers investigate lead quality, pipeline performance and lifecycle trends without reviewing records one by one.

Example prompt: "Which deals created last quarter originated from webinar leads, and how many closed?" The assistant can retrieve the records and examine conversion patterns, provided the attribution data exists.

It has been revealed that setup: HubSpot hosts the server. In your account you create an MCP auth app under Development, then connect an MCP client that supports OAuth 2.1 with PKCE to the HubSpot endpoint. See HubSpot's remote MCP server documentation for current steps.

It has been revealed that access: Unlike a purely analytical server, HubSpot supports selected create and update actions on records such as contacts, companies, deals, tickets and activities. Other objects, including marketing content, are read-only.

Limitations: Available operations differ by object type, and incomplete lead sources or inconsistent lifecycle stages will weaken any analysis.

Best for: B2B marketers and revenue operations teams that manage customers and pipeline in HubSpot.

In a recent development, ahrefs offers a hosted MCP server that brings its SEO data into compatible assistants. It supports conversational research into keywords, backlinks, competing pages and organic visibility, so you can follow up with questions instead of exporting report after report.

Example prompt: "Which websites link to both of our main competitors but don't link to us?" The assistant can retrieve backlink data and help you identify outreach targets, which you can then narrow by Domain Rating or organic traffic.

Industry observers note that setup: According to the Ahrefs MCP documentation, the remote server is available on paid looks starting from Lite, and you authorize it through your AI client. Ahrefs also publishes a getting started guide.

Industry observers note that limitations: Calls made through MCP use your monthly API units in the same way as direct API usage, and rows per request depend on your plan. Ahrefs documents a default cap of 200,000 units per month for keys created through OAuth, which workspace admins can change. The data is also SEO-focused rather than first-party conversion analytics.

Best for: SEO specialists, content marketers and link builders who already use Ahrefs.

Yes, but start with the connections your team actually needs. Each additional server adds tools the assistant has to choose between, which increases complexity. Combining Ahrefs and HubSpot, for example, supports separate SEO and CRM investigations, but connecting several servers does not automatically create a reliable cross-platform reporting system.

Industry observers note that for recurring reports, prepare consistent datasets and validate the first results against your existing dashboards. That catches errors caused by mismatched metrics or attribution rules.

Are MCP servers safe for marketing data? Security depends on the provider, the authentication method and the permissions you grant. Use trusted servers, review access scopes, and enable write operations only when necessary.

In a recent development, do I need coding skills to use MCP servers? Not necessarily. Hosted services usually need less configuration, while local servers such as Google's need extra setup.

Sources indicate that which AI clients support MCP? Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and other tools support MCP connections, though functionality and setup differ.

Recent findings suggest that do MCP servers cost extra? It depends on the provider. Some require paid intends, and others consume API credits or have usage limits.

In a recent development, pick the server that matches the question you ask most often: Google Analytics MCP for GA4 behavior, Coupler for cross-channel reporting, HubSpot for CRM and lifecycle analysis, and Ahrefs for SEO research. Start with read-only access, check usage limits and permissions, and validate early answers against the reports you already trust.

The PyTorch Image Models (timm) library offers a rich collection of state-of-the-art computer vision models, along with useful layers, utilities, optimizers, and data augmentations. With more than 32K GitHub stars and more than 200K daily downloads at the time of writing, it's a go-to resource for image classification and feature extraction for object detection, segmentation, image search, and other downstream tasks.

With pre-trained models covering a wide range of architectures, timm simplifies the workflow for computer vision practitioners.

While 🤗 transformers supports several vision models, timm offers an even broader collection, including many mobile-friendly and efficient models not available in transformers.

The timm integration bridges this gap, bringing the best of both worlds:.

Industry observers note that one of the standout features of the timm integration is that it allows you to leverage the 🤗 pipeline API. The pipeline API abstracts away a lot of complexity, making it easy to load a pre-trained model, perform inference, and view results with a few lines of code.

According to recent reports, let's see how to use a transformers pipeline with the MobileNetV4. This architecture does not have a native transformers implementation, but can be easily used from timm:.

Sources indicate that want to quickly create an interactive web app for image classification? Gradio makes it simple to build a user-friendly interface with minimal code. Let's combine Gradio with the pipeline API to classify food images using a fine-tuned timm ViT model (we will cover fine tuning in a later section).

Here’s how you can set up a quick demo with a timm model:.

It has been revealed that here’s a live example hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. You can test it directly in your browser!

The 🤗 transformers library provides Auto Classes to abstract away the complexity of loading models and processors. With the TimmWrapper, you can use AutoModelForImageClassification and AutoImageProcessor to load any timm model effortlessly.

Recent findings suggest that quantization is a powerful technique to reduce model size and speed up inference, especially for deployment on resource-constrained devices. With the timm integration, you can quantize any timm model on the fly with just a few lines of code using BitsAndBytesConfig from bitsandbytes.

Here’s how simple it is to quantize a timm model:.

Quantized models perform almost identically to full-precision models during inference:.

Fine-tuning a timm model with the Trainer API from 🤗 transformers is straightforward and highly flexible. You can fine-tune your model on custom datasets using the Trainer class, which handles the training loop, logging, and evaluation. Additionally, you can fine-tune using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to train efficiently with fewer parameters.

This section gives a quick overview of both standard fine-tuning and LoRA fine-tuning, with links to the complete code.

The Trainer API makes it easy to set up training with minimal code. Here's an outline of what a fine-tuning setup looks like:.

What's remarkable about this approach is that it mirrors the exact workflow used for native transformers models, maintaining consistency across different model types.

Industry observers note that this means you can use the familiar Trainer API to fine-tune not just Transformers models, but also any timm model—bringing powerful models from the timm library into the Hugging Face ecosystem with minimal adjustments. This significantly broadens the scope of models you can fine-tune using the same trusted tools and workflows.

Model Example:Fine-tuned ViT on Food-101: vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.ft_food101.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) allows you to fine-tune large models efficiently by training only a few additional parameters, rather than the full set of model weights. This makes fine-tuning faster, and allows the use of consumer hardware. You can fine-tune a timm model using LoRA with the PEFT library.

Trainable Parameters with LoRA:.

Model Example:LoRA Fine-Tuned ViT on Food-101: vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.lora_ft_food101.

LoRA is just one example of efficient adapter-based fine-tuning methods you can apply to timm models. The integration of timm with the 🤗 ecosystem opens up a wide variety of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques, allowing you to choose the method that best fits your use case.

Once the model is LoRA fine-tuned, we only push the adapter weights to the Hugging Face Hub. This section helps you to download the adapter weights, merge the adapter weights with the base model, and then perform inference.

It has been revealed that one of Ross' (creator of timm) favourite features is that this integration maintains full 'round-trip' compatibility. Namely, using the wrapper one can fine-tune a timm model on a newly introduced dataset using transformer's Trainer, publish the resulting model to the Hugging Face hub, and then load the fine-tuned model in timm again using timm.create_model('hf-hub:my_org/my_fine_tuned_model', pretrained=True).

Let us see how we can load our fine tuned model ariG23498/vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.ft_food101 with timm.

It has been revealed that with torch.compile in PyTorch 2.0, you can achieve faster inference by compiling your model with just one line of code. The timm integration is fully compatible with torch.compile. Here's a quick benchmark to compare inference time with and without torch.compile using the TimmWrapper.

timm's integration with transformers opens fresh doors for leveraging state-of-the-art vision models with minimal effort. Whether you're looking to fine-tune, quantize, or simply run inference, this integration provides a unified API to streamline your workflow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FriendliAI’s inference infrastructure is now integrated into the Hugging Face Hub as an option in the “Deploy this model” button, simplifying and accelerating generative AI model serving.

Hugging Face empowers developers, researchers, and businesses to innovate in AI. Our common priority is building impactful partnerships that simplify workflows and provide cutting-edge tools for the AI community.

Today, we are excited to announce a partnership between HF and FriendliAI, a leader in accelerated generative AI inference, to enhance how developers deploy and manage AI models. This integration introduces FriendliAI Endpoints as a deployment option within the Hugging Face Hub, offering developers direct access to high-performance, cost-effective inference infrastructure.

In a recent development, friendliAI is ranked as the fastest GPU-based generative AI inference provider by Artificial Analysis, with groundbreaking technologies including continuous batching, native quantization, and best-in-class autoscaling. With this technology, FriendliAI continues to advance the standards for AI inference serving performance, delivering faster processing speeds, reduced latency, and substantial cost savings for deploying generative AI models at scale. Through this partnership, Hugging Face people and FriendliAI customers can effortlessly deploy open-source or custom generative AI models with unparalleled efficiency and reliability.

In a recent development, last year, FriendliAI introduced a Hugging Face integration, enabling consumers to seamlessly deploy Hugging Face models directly within the Friendli Suite platform. Through this integration, users gained access to thousands of supported open-source models on Hugging Face, as well as the capability to deploy private models effortlessly. The list of model architectures currently supported by FriendliAI can be found here.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re taking this integration further by enabling the same capability directly within the Hugging Face Hub, offering 1-click deployment for a seamless user experience. You can deploy models directly from the model card on the Hugging Face Hub using a Friendli Suite account.

According to recent reports, selecting Friendli Endpoints will take you to FriendliAI’s model deployment page. Here, you can deploy the model on NVIDIA H100 GPUs while simultaneously interacting with optimized open-source models. The deployment page features an intuitive interface for setting up Friendli Dedicated Endpoints, the managed service for generative AI inference. Additionally, while your deployment is processing, you can chat with open-source models directly on the page, making it easy to explore and test their capabilities.

With FriendliAI’s advanced GPU-optimized inference engine, Dedicated Endpoints delivers fast and cost-effective inference as a managed service. Developers can effortlessly deploy open-source or custom models on NVIDIA H100 GPUs using Friendli Dedicated Endpoints by clicking “Deploy now” on the model deployment page.

It has been revealed that H100 GPUs are powerful but can be expensive to operate at scale. With FriendliAI’s optimized service, you can reduce the number of GPUs needed while maintaining peak performance, significantly lowering costs. Beyond cost efficiency, Dedicated Endpoints also simplifies the complexities of managing infrastructure.

Sources indicate that friendli Serverless Endpoints is the perfect solution for developers who want to efficiently inference open-source models. This service provides user-friendly APIs for models optimized by FriendliAI, ensuring high performance at a low cost. You can chat with these powerful open-source models directly on the model deployment page.

We’re thrilled to deepen the FriendliAI<>HF collaboration, enhancing accessibility to open-source AI for developers worldwide. FriendliAI’s high-speed, cost-efficient inference solution eliminates the complexities of infrastructure management, empowering people to focus on innovation. Together with FriendliAI, we remain committed to transforming how AI is developed, driving groundbreaking innovation that shapes the next era of AI.

You can also give us a Follow on our organization page to be updated about future news 🔥.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how developers learn, write code, and manage their daily work. Tasks that once required hours of searching, testing, and manual effort can now be completed with help from AI. Developers can use it to understand complex programming concepts, find coding errors, learn upcoming technologies, and complete repetitive tasks.

In a recent development, however, AI is not only useful for writing code faster. It can also help developers improve their technical knowledge, solve problems, and build better learning habits. When used correctly, it can become a useful assistant throughout the software development process.

According to recent reports, the key is to understand where AI can help and where human skills are still needed. Here are several practical ways developers can use AI to improve their learning and productivity.

Learning a newly introduced programming language or understanding a difficult concept can take time. Developers often need to read long explanations, watch tutorials, and test different examples before they understand how something works.

AI can make this process easier by explaining technical concepts in simple language. Instead of searching through several websites, developers can ask direct questions and receive explanations based on their current knowledge.

For example, a developer learning JavaScript can ask AI to explain promises, callbacks, or asynchronous functions. It can break these topics into smaller parts and provide simple code examples to make them easier to understand.

It has been revealed that another useful approach is to ask AI to explain the same concept in different ways. If one explanation is difficult to understand, a different example or comparison may make the idea clearer.

In a recent development, AI explanations are not always accurate, especially when dealing with complex programming concepts or unfamiliar technologies. Developers should verify important information before using it in their projects. Hallucination detection can help identify fabricated facts, incorrect technical explanations, and misleading information in AI-generated responses, making it easier to check the accuracy of what they learn.

This helps developers spend less time struggling with unfamiliar topics and more time building their technical knowledge.

Software development changes regularly. New frameworks, libraries, programming languages, and development methods continue to appear. Developers need to keep learning if they want to stay up to date.

AI can support this process by helping developers create learning aims based on their goals and current skills.

For example, a developer who wants to learn Python can ask AI to create a beginner-friendly learning plan. The plan can include basic syntax, variables, loops, functions, object-oriented programming, and small projects.

According to recent reports, AI can also recommend practical exercises for each topic. Instead of only reading about a programming concept, developers can write code and test their understanding.

Here are some ways to use AI when learning upcoming technologies:.

Industry observers note that however, developers should not depend entirely on AI-generated explanations. They should also read official documentation and test examples themselves. This helps them understand how technologies work in real development environments.

AI can help developers improve their coding skills by providing examples, explaining different solutions, and identifying areas that need improvement.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a developer may write a function that works but contains unnecessary steps. They can ask AI to review the code and suggest ways to make it easier to read, maintain, or understand.

AI can also explain why one solution may be better than another. This allows developers to learn different approaches instead of always following the first solution they find.

Some practical ways to use AI for coding improvement include:.

Industry observers note that developers can also ask AI to create small coding challenges based on their skill level. For example, someone learning Python can request exercises about lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions.

The vital thing is to understand the code instead of copying it without review. Developers who examine the logic behind each solution can improve their programming knowledge over time.

Sources indicate that developers learn newly introduced information from many sources, including online courses, technical blogs, documentation, tutorials, and coding projects. Without a proper system, it can become difficult to find useful information when they need it again.

AI can help developers organize this knowledge and make learning resources easier to review.

For example, developers can use AI to summarize long technical explanations, create revision questions, and organize important programming concepts into smaller topics. They can also turn their learning notes into structured study guides that make it easier to revisit important information.

According to recent reports, A well-organized knowledge system can be useful when learning a upcoming framework or preparing for technical interviews. Instead of searching through old browser tabs or reading the same documentation repeatedly, developers can return to their saved explanations and notes.

Here are some useful ways to organize technical knowledge:.

Technical documentation can contain detailed explanations that are difficult to remember. Developers can use AI to summarize notable sections and turn them into short notes.

For example, when learning a new API, they can save information about its main functions, parameters, common errors, and practical examples.

Reading information does not always mean remembering it. Developers can ask AI to create questions from their notes so they can test their understanding.

For example, after learning about database indexing, they can create questions about how indexes work, when to use them, and how they affect query performance.

In a recent development, developers should also save crucial information about their projects. This may include coding decisions, API details, database structures, and solutions to common problems.

Keeping these details organized makes it easier to return to a project after a break or help another developer understand the work.

In a recent development, developers spend a large part of their working time on tasks that do not always require complex problem-solving. These may include writing basic code structures, creating test cases, preparing documentation, and handling repeated coding patterns.

AI can help reduce this manual effort by generating suggestions and automating parts of these tasks.

It has been revealed that for example, when starting a new project, developers often need to create similar code structures, such as basic functions, configuration files, and reusable components. An AI coding assistant can generate an initial version that developers can review and adjust.

Automating these activities gives developers more time to focus on vital parts of their projects, such as system design, complex features, and problem-solving.

Recent findings suggest that however, generated code should always be checked before it is added to a project. Developers need to make sure it follows project requirements, coding standards, and security rules.

Finding and fixing bugs is an vital part of software development. Even experienced developers can spend hours trying to understand why a program is not working as expected.

AI can help make debugging easier by explaining error messages, identifying possible causes, and suggesting solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters a Python error, they can share the relevant code and error message with an AI assistant. The assistant can explain what the error means and suggest possible ways to fix it.

According to recent reports, AI can also help developers review code before submitting it. It may identify common challenges such as:.

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain why a particular bug occurs instead of only requesting a corrected version of the code.

This helps developers understand the problem and avoid making the same mistake in future projects.

Still, AI suggestions are not always correct. Developers should test proposed fixes, review the surrounding code, and confirm that the solution does not introduce new problems.

It has been revealed that managing several development tasks at once can be difficult. Developers may need to work on fresh features, fix bugs, review code, attend meetings, and meet project deadlines.

AI can help organize these responsibilities by breaking large tasks into smaller and more manageable steps.

For example, if a developer needs to build a user authentication system, they can ask AI to divide the work into separate tasks. These may include creating registration forms, setting up database tables, implementing login logic, adding password protection, and testing the system.

This makes it easier to understand the work involved and decide what needs attention first.

According to recent reports, AI can also help explain technical requirements before development begins. This may reduce confusion and help developers identify missing details early.

However, AI-generated plans should be treated as starting points. Developers still need to consider their actual deadlines, technical limitations, and project requirements before following them.

Although AI offers many benefits, depending on it for every programming task can affect a developer's ability to solve problems independently.

If developers always ask AI to write code, fix errors, and explain every concept, they may miss opportunities to develop their own technical skills.

A 2026 Anthropic study found that participants using AI scored 17 percentage points lower on a programming knowledge quiz than participants who worked without AI in the experiment. This highlights why understanding the work still matters when using coding assistants.

Developers can avoid excessive dependence on AI by following a few simple practices:.

It has been revealed that when facing a coding problem, spend some time understanding it and trying possible solutions. If you get stuck, use AI to explore the issue rather than asking it to complete everything.

Never add AI-generated code to a project without understanding what it does. Review the logic, check the functions, and test the output.

AI can sometimes provide outdated information, incorrect code, or explanations that do not fit a particular project. Check vital details against official documentation and reliable technical resources.

In a recent development, regular coding practice without assistance helps developers maintain their problem-solving skills. It also reveals whether they truly understand a programming concept.

The best approach is to use AI as a helpful assistant while keeping independent thinking and technical judgment at the center of development work.

Using AI occasionally can be helpful, but developers can get more value from it by making it part of a regular learning and working routine.

A simple daily routine can help developers balance their project responsibilities with continuous learning.

For example, developers can follow this approach:.

Start with a learning goal: Spend some time understanding a upcoming programming concept, framework, or technology. Use AI to explain difficult topics and provide practical examples.

Initiative the day's development tasks: Ask AI to help organize important tasks and break complex work into smaller steps.

Use AI during development: Get help with unfamiliar code, debugging, test cases, and repetitive tasks. Review all suggestions before using them.

Save useful information: Keep important explanations, coding examples, and solutions in an organized knowledge base for future reference.

Review what you learned: At the end of the day, revisit important concepts and test your understanding through small questions or coding exercises.

According to recent reports, developers do not need to spend hours following this routine. Even a short period of focused learning each day can help them build knowledge while managing their regular development work.

It has been revealed that AI is becoming a useful part of modern software development. It can help developers understand difficult concepts, learn fresh technologies, improve code quality, debug problems, and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.

According to recent reports, however, better productivity does not simply mean writing more code in less time. Developers also need to understand what they are building, improve their problem-solving skills, and keep learning as technology changes.

The most effective approach is to use AI for support rather than letting it make every decision. By combining AI assistance with regular practice, independent thinking, and organized learning, developers can improve both their technical skills and everyday productivity.

SmolVLM Grows Smaller – Introducing the 256M & 500M Models!

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re excited to announce two new additions to the SmolVLM family: SmolVLM-256M and SmolVLM-500M.
  • Recent findings suggest that we built on everything we learned from SmolVLM 2B while focusing on efficiency, data mixtures, and upcoming design trade-offs.
  • Recent findings suggest that this release comes with four checkpoints: two base models and two instruction fine-tuned models with sizes 256M and 500M parameters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we’re excited to announce two new additions to the SmolVLM family: SmolVLM-256M and SmolVLM-500M. That’s right—256M parameters, making it the smallest Vision Language Model in the world!

Recent findings suggest that we built on everything we learned from SmolVLM 2B while focusing on efficiency, data mixtures, and upcoming design trade-offs. We are excited to introduce a pair of models that preserve strong multimodal performance in a fraction of the footprint.

Recent findings suggest that this release comes with four checkpoints: two base models and two instruction fine-tuned models with sizes 256M and 500M parameters. These models can be loadable directly to transformers, MLX and ONNX, and we have demos for transformers and WebGPU (with ONNX). You can find all the models and the demo for this release here.

We're now reaching model parity with the SmolLM2 family (135M, 360M, 1.7B), so you have a complete set of smaller LLM + VLM combos to play with.

When we released SmolVLM 2B, the community response was fantastic: The model is very light weight, open-source and permissive, and easy to integrate into existing workflows. But we wanted to push this approach even further for people working with constrained devices, consumer laptops, or even potentially browser-based inference. That’s where our latest 256M and 500M models come in. On the other side, for people trying to process huge amounts of data, these models can run at a fraction of the cost of the 2B model.

According to recent reports, in the last year, we trained two 80B VLMs and reduced them to 8B. Then for SmolVLM we took the challenge of reducing that 2B. And what we learned was that we could push the frontier way further! We are excited to show that at 256M and 500M we can still get great performance. Our newly introduced 256M model is the smallest VLM ever released, yet it surpasses the performance of our Idefics 80B model from just 17 months ago.

Industry observers note that with just 256 million parameters, this model stands as the tiniest VLM ever. Despite its small size, it packs a surprising punch. It’s more than capable on many multimodal tasks, including:.

Sources indicate that if you need more performance headroom while still keeping the memory usage low, SmolVLM-500M is our half-billion-parameter compromise. It’s significantly smaller than the previous 2B release yet manages to push scores on tasks like DocVQA and MMMU closer to the bigger models. We also found this model to be more robust to prompting, which makes it out-of-the-box better fitted for production. But both models do great when fine-tuned.

We have visualized the throughput gains across different batch sizes in below graph. Below numbers are throughput benchmarks ran on A100.

1. Vision Encoder Choices Previously, we used the standard SigLIP 400M SO vision backbone, the same one found in many VLM architectures. For these smaller models, we experimented with two setups:.

In a recent development, we found the performance gap wasn’t significant enough to justify the heavier encoder for our 256M and 500M models. So, we decided to go small on the vision encoder, too. As a bonus, the smaller encoder processes images at a larger resolution, which (per research from Apple and Google) can often yield better visual understanding without ballooning parameter counts.

Similarly to our previous release, we rely on The Cauldron and Docmatix with the addition of MathWriting to the mix.

The proportions of the datasets were adjusted to place a stronger emphasis on document understanding (41%) and image captioning (14%), while still maintaining a balanced focus on other essential areas such as visual reasoning, chart comprehension, and general instruction following. With this patch the model is built on a strong document understanding basis and lets the door open to fine-tunes that will adjust its understanding of specific tasks.

We increased the pixel shuffle even more! Our upcoming models encode images at a rate of 4096 pixels per token, compared to 1820 pixels per token in the 2B model.

According to recent reports, to optimize the tokenization even more, we added special tokens to represent our sub-image separators in a more efficient way. This means that now instead of a string like being mapped to 7 tokens, it is mapped to a single token. We did the same for strings up to . This led to a sizeable improvement in the model's stability during training and quality of the results. More details were documented in this LinkedIn post.

Industry observers note that 4. Completing the SmolLM2-SmolVLM family.

SmolLM2 came in three sizes: 135M, 360M, and 1.7B. With the two models we are releasing today, we now have a complete set of smaller LLM + VLM combos to play with.

Recent findings suggest that we also found that it's surprisingly easy to fine-tune and experiment. The team behind the ColBERT-like retrieval models have trained ColSmolVLM, delivering SOTA multimodal retrieval speeds with performance rivaling models 10x their size. SmolVLM makes it faster and cheaper to build searchable databases. We think the 256M model can become a great specialized model for many tasks. Find the link on how to use the latest ColSmolVLM with the new SmolVLM models in Next Steps.

Industry observers note that we partnered with IBM to build models for Docling. Their early results with the 256M model are impressive. Below are some early examples they shared with us. Stay tuned for more updates on this!

Newer SmolVLMs are working out-of-the-box with the old SmolVLM code, so you can use transformers and MLX for inference and fine-tuning, and TRL for alignment 🚀 Moreover, this release also comes with ONNX checkpoints.

#149705. Latest Update: Mastering Long Contexts in LLMs with KVPress

📅 23 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Mastering Long Contexts in LLMs with KVPress

📅 23 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: KVPress packs the latest KV cache compression techniques, enabling memory-efficient long-context LLMs.
  • In a recent development, one of the key features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their context window—the maximum number of tokens they can process in a single request.
  • Larger context windows unlock incredible possibilities:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: KVPress packs the latest KV cache compression techniques, enabling memory-efficient long-context LLMs. 🚀.

In a recent development, one of the key features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their context window—the maximum number of tokens they can process in a single request. As LLMs evolve, their context windows are becoming increasingly larger.

Larger context windows unlock incredible possibilities:.

However, these extended windows come at a cost—memory taken by the long context in the KV Cache becomes hard to manage. For instance, handling 1M tokens with Llama 3-70B in float16 demands 330GB for KV Cache, rendering it infeasible for many applications.

In this blog post, we'll address one solution for this problem: compressing the KV Cache for more efficient generation. To achieve this, we'll explore:.

Before getting started, explore KVPress in this Space (you'll find examples at the end if needed):.

Figure 1: Key Value cache inside the attention module (Source: NVIDIA).

In autoregressive models, text generation happens token by token, with each prediction relying on all preceding tokens for context. For example:.

In a recent development, this repetitive computation becomes inefficient as the sequence grows, especially for large models. KV Cache optimizes this process by storing the intermediate results—keys (K) and values (V)—from the attention layers, so the model can reuse them for future tokens instead of recalculating them.

As powerful as the KV Cache is, it comes with a major drawback-it scales linearly with the size of the context window. While this might not sound alarming at first, let's break it down to see why this becomes a serious bottleneck.

The values stored in the KV Cache come from all the attention blocks used by the model. Therefore, its size depends on the model architecture, which dictates the number of attention heads. More concretely, the memory consumed by the KV Cache is determined by the following equation:.

Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers×nheads×d×ntokens \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times \text{precision} \times n_{layers} \times n_{heads} \times d \times n_{tokens} Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers​×nheads​×d×ntokens​.

In a recent development, each of these factors contributes to the explosion in memory usage. To make this more tangible, let's consider a concrete example—Llama 3-70B running in bfloat16 precision (as recommended by the model authors) with a context size of 1M tokens:.

Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1M = 327.6 \text{GB} Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB.

It has been revealed that since bfloat16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, the model weights alone require 140 GB (70B x 2 bytes). This means that running the model with a 1M token context size demands approximately 470 GB of memory, with the KV cache alone accounting for a staggering 70% of this total.

As we've seen, the KV Cache is both a critical enabler and a significant bottleneck for deploying large language models (LLMs) with long context windows. Addressing the linearly scaling memory problem requires innovative compression techniques, and that's exactly where KVPress steps in.

Sources indicate that KVPress, developed by NVIDIA, is a Python toolkit designed to address the memory challenges of large KV Caches by providing a suite of state-of-the-art compression techniques. It also integrates with other approaches, such as KV Cache Quantization, a method built into the transformers library to reduce memory usage (the precision term in the equation above), further expanding its utility (details here).

In a recent development, for researchers specializing in compression, KVPress offers a flexible and modular framework, making it easy to understand and extend with new methods. For developers, KVPress simplifies the process of deploying these cutting-edge techniques, enabling quick and efficient integration into real-world applications.

At its core, KVPress leverages presses, which are advanced compression algorithms specifically designed to reduce the memory footprint of the KV Cache.

According to recent reports, many of these presses rely on a score that is used in each head to prune the KV pairs with the lowest importance. For instance the KnormPress prunes the KV pairs with lowest key value norm (paper), and SnapKVPress prunes the KV pairs associated with a low attention weights for the latest queries (paper).

These presses are seamlessly integrated into the attention layers of the model using forward hooks.

Figure 2: KV Compression visualized (Source: NVIDIA).

During text generation, they dynamically compress the KV Cache, reducing memory usage without compromising the model's ability to generate coherent and accurate outputs. Each press is characterized by a compression_ratio attribute, which determines the degree of compression applied to the KV Cache.

These presses integrate seamlessly with a custom transformers pipeline, enabling easy application and experimentation.

Sources indicate that here's how you can use a press with KVPress with one of the many presses, ExpectedAttentionPress. This press prunes the KV pairs associated with the lowest expected attention weight for future queries.

Try using it directly in this Hugging Face space or in this Google colab notebook!

By targeting the pre-filling phase, KVPress ensures that the cache is compressed when it's largest—helping reduce memory overhead for sequences with tens of thousands or even millions of tokens.

Recent findings suggest that the plot below demonstrates the GPU memory savings achieved with KVPress compression as prompt lengths increase. For shorter prompts, most of the memory is allocated to model weights—approximately 15GB for Llama 3.1 8B in bfloat16. However, as prompt lengths grow, the KV cache becomes a major contributor to memory consumption. For 128k context length, applying KVPress with a 50% compression ratio reduces peak memory usage from 45GB to 37GB. This smaller KV cache also improves decoding speed, from 11 tokens per second to 17 tokens per second on an A100 GPU (source). .

Figure 3: Memory usage vs Context length (Source: NVIDIA).

According to recent reports, the research community has been actively developing various techniques for KV cache compression. KVPress encourages researchers to contribute their methods and already provides more than a dozen presses.

In a recent development, to evaluate the performance of these presses, KVPress includes a simple CLI for benchmarking them on standard long-context datasets such as RULER, InfiniteBench, and Loogle. The plot below benchmarks 9 different presses on the RULER dataset with 4k context length and different compression ratio. The best performing press on this dataset is a combination of the AdaKVPress (paper) and ExpectedAttentionPress, a upcoming unpublished pruning technique created by the authors of KVPress (more information here).

Figure 4: Average score vs Compression ratio (Source: NVIDIA).

The growing context windows of LLMs unlock newly introduced possibilities but pose significant memory challenges with the linearly scaling KV Cache. KVPress addresses this by compressing the cache during the critical pre-filling phase.

It has been revealed that while KVPress improves memory efficiency, higher compression ratios can impact model accuracy, as shown in the benchmark plot. Further research is needed to develop more effective compression algorithms that minimize trade-offs.

With its seamless integration into the transformers library and modular design, KVPress empowers researchers and developers to handle long-context LLMs efficiently and design upcoming compression techniques. It's a practical solution for scaling LLMs without overwhelming memory resources—ensuring innovation stays accessible as models grow.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We have added vision support to smolagents, which unlocks the use of vision language models in agentic pipelines natively.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Matthew 7, 3-5.

We have added vision support to smolagents, which unlocks the use of vision language models in agentic pipelines natively.

In the agentic world, many capabilities are hidden behind a vision wall. A common example is web browsing: web pages feature rich visual content that you never fully recover by simply extracting their text, be it the relative position of objects, messages transmitted through color, specific icons… In this case, vision is a real superpower for agents. So we just added this capability to our smolagents!

Teaser of what this gives: an agentic browser that navigates the web in complete autonomy!

Here's an example of what it looks like:.

🤔 How do we want to pass images to agents? Passing an image can be done in two ways:.

For the case where we want to pass images at once, we added the possibility to pass a list of images to the agent in the run method: agent.run("Describe these images:", images=[image_1, image_2]) .

These image inputs are then stored in the task_images attribute of TaskStep along with the prompt of the task that you'd like to accomplish.

Recent findings suggest that when running the agent, they will be passed to the model. This comes in handy with cases like taking actions based on long PDFs that include visual elements.

How to dynamically add images into the agent’s memory?

To find out, we first need to understand how our agents work.

All agents in smolagents are based on the singular MultiStepAgent class, which is an abstraction of the ReAct framework. On a basic level, this class performs actions on a cycle of following steps, where existing variables and knowledge are incorporated into the agent logs as follows:.

The figure below details this process:.

As you can see, for use cases where images are dynamically retrieved (e.g. web browser agent), we support adding images to the model’s ActionStep, in attribute step_log.observation_images.

This can be done via a callback, which will be run at the end of each step.

Let's demonstrate how to make such a callback, and using it to build a web browser agent.👇👇.

We’re going to use helium. It provides browser automations based on selenium: this will be an easier way for our agent to manipulate webpages.

According to recent reports, the agent itself can use helium directly, so no need for specific tools: it can directly use helium to perform actions, such as click("top 10") to click the button named "top 10" visible on the page. We still have to make some tools to help the agent navigate the web: a tool to go back to the previous page, and another tool to close pop-ups, because these are quite hard to grab for helium since they don’t have any text on their close buttons.

Industry observers note that for now, the agent has no visual input. So let us demonstrate how to dynamically feed it images in its step logs by using a callback. We make a callback save_screenshot that will be run at the end of each step.

The most vital line here is when we add the image in our observations images: step_log.observations_images = [image.copy()].

Recent findings suggest that this callback accepts both the step_log, and the agent itself as arguments. Having agent as an input allows to perform deeper operations than just modifying the last logs.

Let's make a model. We've added support for images in all models. Just one precision: when using TransformersModel with a VLM, for it to work properly you need to pass flatten_messages_as_text as False upon initialization, like:.

For this demo, let's use a bigger Qwen2VL via Fireworks API:.

Sources indicate that now let’s move on to defining our agent. We set the highest verbosity_level to display the LLM’s full output messages to view its thoughts, and we increased max_steps to 20 to give the agent more steps to explore the web. We also provide it with our callback save_screenshot defined above.

Finally, we provide our agent with some guidance about using helium.

Now everything's ready: Let’s run our agent!

Recent findings suggest that note, however, that this task is really hard: depending on the VLM that you use, this might not always work. Strong VLMs like Qwen2VL-72B or GPT-4o succeed more often.

This will give you a glimpse of the capabilities of a vision-enabled CodeAgent, but there’s much more to do!

We are looking forward to seeing what you will build with vision language models and smolagents!

Note: for the modal closing selectors please note that modals are also known as dialog elements and if built robustly should have a role="dialog" attribute in this is something that can be searched for when identifying these pop up windows.

In addition, any dialog/modal window should be closeable via the escape key as well!

Hope this helps identify modals/dialogs in a broader sense and/or helps close them out easier!

How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad.
  • It has been revealed that motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

It has been revealed that motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells people where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Industry observers note that motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

Recent findings suggest that it directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a fresh user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a upcoming view slides in from the right, a short transition demonstrates consumers where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It has been revealed that it confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, people repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help newly introduced customers reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: people settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

In a recent development, animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets people grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

In a recent development, the right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:.

In a recent development, CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

Recent findings suggest that the Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

In a recent development, lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm customers. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

Sources indicate that for performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:.

Industry observers note that beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

According to recent reports, motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your upcoming owners and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

According to recent reports, the best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where customers most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.
