With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ newly introduced publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

Recent findings suggest that the difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

3 weeks ago, we indicated how hard it is to correctly evaluate LLM performance on math problems, and introduced Math-Verify, a better solution to validate models on math (read more in the announcement)!

Today, we’re thrilled to share that we’ve used Math-Verify to thoroughly re-evaluate all 3,751 models ever submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard, for even fairer and more robust model comparisons!

The Open LLM Leaderboard is the most used leaderboard on the Hugging Face Hub: it compares open Large Language Models (LLM) performance across various tasks. One of these tasks, called MATH-Hard, is specifically about math problems: it evaluates how well LLMs solve high-school and university-level math problems. It uses 1,324 highest difficulty problems (Level 5) from the Hendrycks MATH dataset spread across 7 topics (precalculus, prealgebra, algebra, intermediate algebra, counting/probability and number theory), using a 5-shot approach (the model is provided with 5 examples in the prompt to showcase how it should answer).

A typical question looks like this:.

In the leaderboard, models would have to end their answers with a very specific string (following the Minerva-Math paper):.

The leaderboard would then try to parse [ANSWER] with SymPy to convert it to a symbolic representation (and simplify the values if needed), before finally comparing it to the gold target.

However, customers reported a number of issues with the above.

To start, a recurring problem was the inability of some models to follow the expected answer format from the examples: they outputted other sentences instead to introduce their answers. Since the format was not followed, answers were marked as wrong even if they were actually correct! (Which is an issue if what you’re interested in is “how good the model is at math” specifically).

The next step, converting [ANSWER] to the symbolic representation also presented some concerns, this time linked to the SymPy parsing:.

On the final step, when comparing the extracted answer with the target expression, a number of concerns also occurred:.

All of these issues are now completely fixed with the new Math-Verify parser!

Recent findings suggest that as all these problems tend to accumulate, some models deeply suffered from this, and their performance was strongly underestimated… so we removed the previous evaluator and added Math-Verify, which was as simple as changing only 3 lines of code! (You can try it too on your math evals!).

This therefore meant re-evaluating all submitted models since June… and it completely overhauled the top 20 models on the MATH subset of the leaderboard.

On average, models solved 61 more problems across the board, equating to a 4.66-point increase across the board!

The two subsets that showed the most significant improvement were both algebra-related (Algebra and Prealgebra) with gains of 8.27 and 6.93, respectively. In extreme cases, some models demonstrated improvements of nearly 90 points on these subsets. We believe these subsets saw the greatest improvement because they frequently involve answers presented as sets (due to questions with multiple solutions) and matrices. The Math-Verify has enhanced its handling of both answer types, contributing to these notable gains.

In a recent development, we initially discovered the math evaluation issues when inspecting Qwen models, which had unusually low scores compared to the self-reported performance. After the Math-Verify introduction, the scores more than doubled for these models, showcasing previous severe underestimation of performance.

But Qwen models aren’t alone. Another major family affected is DeepSeek. After switching to Math-Verify, DeepSeek models almost tripled their scores! This is because their answers are typically wrapped in boxed (\boxed{}) notations which the old evaluator couldn’t extract.

Sources indicate that as mentioned at the beginning, the Top 20 rankings have undergone a significant shift, with Nvidia’s AceMath models now dominating the MATH-Hard leaderboard. Other major beneficiaries of this change are the Qwen derivatives, which are now almost exclusively the only models ranking right below AceMath. Following is the complete table comparing the old and upcoming Top 20 leaderboard rankings:.

Finally, we examined how the overall Leaderboard results have evolved. While the top four positions remain unchanged, the rest have undergone significant shifts. Due to the rise of multiple Qwen derivatives in the MATH subset, the presence of Qwen models among the top 20 has grown-derived models grown even further at the Overall results.

It has been revealed that many other models also completely jumped in the rankings, gaining 200 places or more! You can check out the results in more detail at the Open LLM Leaderboard.

It has been revealed that the introduction of Math-Verify has significantly improved the accuracy and fairness of our evaluations on the Open LLM Leaderboard. This has led to a reshuffling of the leaderboard, with many models showing substantial improvements in their scores.

We encourage all developers and researchers to adopt Math-Verify for their own math evaluations. By doing so, you can ensure that your models are evaluated with more reliable results. Additionally, we invite you to explore the updated rankings and see how your favorite models have changed in performance.

Recent findings suggest that A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame. Today several tools produce 1080p or even 4K clips with synchronized audio, camera control and reference-based consistency. The market also moves swiftly: OpenAI declared it was shutting down Sora in March 2026, so the list of tools worth using has changed.

This guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today. For each one you will see what it does well, where it falls short and who it suits. Looks, credits and model names change often, so confirm details on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Industry observers note that openArt’s AI video generator puts a range of video models behind one interface. Its page lists models such as Veo 3.1, Kling, Seedance, Wan, Hailuo and PixVerse, so you can run the same prompt on different engines and compare the results without managing separate accounts.

According to recent reports, beyond text-to-video and image-to-video, it offers start and end frame control, video-to-video restyling, motion transfer from a reference clip, a character builder for consistency, lip sync and conversational editing for tasks such as swapping a background or relighting a scene. Resolution goes up to 4K on many models, with 1080p as the default, and clips are usually up to 15 seconds, with longer limits on a few models.

Strengths: model variety, a single credit pool, editing tools alongside generation and a shared library for your clips.

In a recent development, limits: credit use varies by model, so it is worth testing short clips first. Commercial-use rights depend on your initiative and on the model you pick, so check the pricing and terms pages.

Best for: creators and small teams that want to compare models promptly instead of committing to one.

According to recent reports, veo is Google DeepMind’s video model. Veo 3.1 generates sound effects, ambient noise and dialogue together with the video, supports image-to-video, first and last frame transitions, reference images for characters or objects, and outputs 1080p and 4K. You can reach it through the Gemini app, Google Flow and the Gemini API.

Strengths: audio generated with the picture, strong prompt adherence and an API that fits into developer workflows.

According to recent reports, limits: base clips are short, around 8 seconds, so longer scenes rely on scene extension. Dialogue quality in short segments is still being refined, and access and quotas depend on your Google strategy.

Best for: developers and marketers who want audio and video from one prompt, or who proposal to automate generation through an API.

Runway has been a staple of AI filmmaking since its early Gen models. Its pricing page lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph alongside partner models, and the paid plans include all video and image models, 4K upscaling and parallel generations. Higher tiers add features such as voice clones, brand kits and HDR or ProRes output.

Strengths: polished editing tools, video-to-video workflows and a professional output pipeline that suits post-production teams.

Limits: credits are consumed promptly on premium models, and on the lower paid aims they do not roll over from month to month.

Best for: video editors and agencies that need control over shots and want AI to fit into an existing editing process.

According to recent reports, kling from Kuaishou has built a reputation for natural motion and expressive characters. The current release, Kling 4.0, sits alongside tools such as Motion Control, a canvas workspace, an agent and MCP or CLI batch generation for teams that want to automate production.

Strengths: realistic movement, motion transfer and batch tools for producing many short clips.

Recent findings suggest that limits: the main site does not spell out all clip-length and resolution limits for each model, so check the model page you initiative to use. Pricing and free credits vary by region and plan.

Best for: social video, product shots and character-driven clips where motion quality is the priority.

Luma’s Dream Machine is built on the Ray model family. Its current page lists Ray3.2 and Ray3.14, along with a “Modify video” tool that restyles footage, extends duration and reframes aspect ratios. It also lists camera-motion controls and high-quality EXR export for professional pipelines.

Strengths: reshooting or restyling existing footage, camera-motion control and pipeline-friendly export.

Limits: paid aims start at around $30 per month (or less when billed yearly), and heavy use pushes you into the higher tiers.

Best for: filmmakers and designers who want to modify and extend footage rather than only generate new clips.

Sources indicate that adobe Firefly offers text-to-video and image-to-video with Adobe’s own Firefly Video Model. It also provides partner models, including Google Veo 3.1, Luma Ray3, Kling and Runway Gen-4.5, so you can compare outputs from inside one product. An Assembler and AI video editor let you trim, reorder, extend and add voiceovers, music and sound effects.

Recent findings suggest that adobe states that the Firefly Video Model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain material, and describes its output as safe for commercial use. Partner models may carry different terms, so read the details for whichever model you choose.

Strengths: a clear licensing story for the native model, integration with Adobe’s creative apps and an included editor.

According to recent reports, limits: most clips run up to 8 seconds, with some models reaching 15. Credits are allocated monthly, and premium partner models can use them faster.

Best for: brand and in-house teams that care about provenance and already work in Adobe tools.

In a recent development, the table summarizes what each vendor’s own pages say at the time of writing. “Entry paid blueprint” figures are US prices billed annually where the vendor offers that option.

Credit counts are hard to compare, so convert them to clips. Runway’s pricing page lists Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per 5-second clip, which means the 625 monthly credits on the Standard plan cover roughly ten clips. Adobe says its Standard plan’s 2,000 credits equal up to 40 five-second videos, and OpenArt’s Starter plan lists about 50 videos for 4,000 credits. Premium models cost more: the same Runway page lists Aleph 2.0 at 140 credits per 5 seconds.

According to recent reports, initiative for waste. If you keep one usable clip out of every three attempts, your real cost per finished shot is about three times the sticker price. Test with short, low-resolution drafts, then render the winner at full quality.

Recent findings suggest that because every tool outputs short clips, the real work is assembly. A typical workflow is: write a shot list, generate two or three takes per shot, pick the best, normalize them to one format, join them and add captions and audio. FFmpeg handles the joining step from the command line:.

According to recent reports, matching resolution, frame rate and codec before joining avoids glitches at the cut points. For character consistency across shots, reuse the same reference image in every prompt and keep descriptions of the subject identical.

If the clip ends up on your own site, treat it like any other media. Provide a poster image, load metadata only until the visitor presses play, and include captions so deaf and hard-of-hearing owners, and anyone watching without sound, can follow along. The W3C’s guidance on captions and subtitles explains what to include, and the MDN video element reference covers the attributes below.

It has been revealed that also write a text description or transcript near the video. Search engines and screen reader owners cannot see the footage, so the surrounding text is what explains it.

According to recent reports, short, structured prompts beat long, vague ones. Describe the elements in the order a director would:.

Change one element at a time between takes so you can tell which change improved the result.

According to recent reports, marketing demos show the best of a tool, so run your own test. Use the same prompt, duration and aspect ratio on each tool, generate a few takes and score them against a short checklist. Keep notes on how many credits each usable clip costs.

Run the same test again with an image-to-video input if your workflow starts from product photos or illustrations. That often exposes differences in consistency that text prompts hide.

Sources indicate that which AI video generator is best? There is no single winner. Veo is strong for audio, Runway for editing, Kling for motion, Luma for modifying footage and Firefly for licensing clarity. A multi-model tool such as OpenArt helps you compare them.

Can AI video generators make long videos? Not in one pass. Most models create short clips, so longer videos are built by extending or stitching clips together.

It has been revealed that is Sora still available? OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it was shutting down the Sora app and API, so it is not a safe choice for upcoming projects.

It has been revealed that can I use AI videos commercially? Often, but it depends on the strategy and the underlying model. Read the current terms before publishing.

Sources indicate that how do I keep a character consistent across clips? Reuse the same reference image, keep the subject description identical in every prompt, and use character or reference tools where the platform offers them.

According to recent reports, should I add captions to AI-generated video? Yes. Captions help accessibility and viewers watching without sound, and they give search engines text to index.

Industry observers note that do I need a powerful computer? No. These services run in the cloud, so a browser and a stable connection are enough.

The best AI video generator depends on what you make. Start with a short test prompt, compare a few tools, and keep the one that gives you usable clips at a sensible credit cost. If you are not sure where to begin, a multi-model option such as OpenArt lets you try several engines before you settle on one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last December, Google released PaliGemma 2: a fresh family of pre-trained (pt) PaliGemma vision language models (VLMs) based on SigLIP and Gemma 2. The models come in three different sizes (3B, 10B, 28B) and three different resolutions (224x224, 448x448, 896x896).

Today, Google is releasing PaliGemma 2 mix: fine-tuned on a mix of vision language tasks, including OCR, long and short captioning and more.

PaliGemma 2 pretrained (pt) variants are great vision language models to transfer on a given task at hand. All pt checkpoints are meant to be fine-tuned on a downstream task and were released for that purpose.

The mix models give a quick idea of the performance one would get when fine-tuning the pre-trained checkpoints on a downstream task. The main purpose of the PaliGemma model family is to provide pretrained models that can learn better on a downstream task, instead of providing a versatile chat model. Mix models give a good signal of how pt models perform when fine-tuned on a mix of academic datasets.

You can read more about PaliGemma 2 in this blog post.

You can find all the mix models and the demo in this collection.

When prompting PaliGemma 2 mix models, we can use open-ended prompts. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere.
  • We are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere. Our goal is simple: make video understanding accessible across all devices and use cases, from phones to servers.

We are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero. We've made all models and demos available in this collection.

Industry observers note that want to try SmolVLM2 right away? Check out our interactive chat interface where you can test visual and video understanding capabilities of SmolVLM2 2.2B through a simple, intuitive interface.

We are introducing three latest models with 256M, 500M and 2.2B parameters. The 2.2B model is the go-to choice for vision and video tasks, while the 500M and 256M models represent the smallest video language models ever released.

It has been revealed that while they're small in size, they outperform any existing models per memory consumption. Looking at Video-MME (the go-to scientific benchmark in video), SmolVLM2 joins frontier model families on the 2B range and we lead the pack in the even smaller space.

Video-MME stands out as a comprehensive benchmark due to its extensive coverage across diverse video types, varying durations (11 seconds to 1 hour), multiple data modalities (including subtitles and audio), and high-quality expert annotations spanning 900 videos totaling 254 hours. Learn more here.

Compared with the previous SmolVLM family, our new 2.2B model got better at solving math problems with images, reading text in photos, understanding complex diagrams, and tackling scientific visual questions. This reveals in the model performance across different benchmarks:.

Sources indicate that when it comes to video tasks, 2.2B is a good bang for the buck. Across the various scientific benchmarks we evaluated it on, we want to highlight its performance on Video-MME where it outperforms all existing 2B models.

We were able to achieve a good balance on video/image performance thanks to the data mixture learnings published in Apollo: An Exploration of Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models.

It’s so memory efficient, that you can run it even in a free Google Colab.

Nobody dared to release such small video models until today.

Our new SmolVLM2-500M-Video-Instruct model has video capabilities very close to SmolVLM 2.2B, but at a fraction of the size: we're getting the same video understanding capabilities with less than a quarter of the parameters 🤯.

Recent findings suggest that and then there's our little experiment, the SmolVLM2-256M-Video-Instruct. Think of it as our "what if" project - what if we could push the boundaries of small models even further? Taking inspiration from what IBM achieved with our base SmolVLM-256M-Instruct a few weeks ago, we wanted to see how far we could go with video understanding. While it's more of an experimental release, we're hoping it'll inspire some creative applications and specialized fine-tuning projects.

To demonstrate our vision in small video models, we've built three practical applications that showcase the versatility of these models.

We make SmolVLM2 available to use with transformers and MLX from day zero. In this section, you can find different inference alternatives and tutorials for video and multiple images.

SigLIP 2: A better multilingual vision language encoder

📅 21 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that today Google releases a new and better family of multilingual vision-language encoders, SigLIP 2.
  • SigLIP 2 models outperform the older SigLIP ones at all model scales in core capabilities, including zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and transfer performance when extracting visual representations for Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
  • A cherry on top is the dynamic resolution (naflex) variant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today Google releases a new and better family of multilingual vision-language encoders, SigLIP 2. The authors have extended the training objective of SigLIP (sigmoid loss) with additional objectives for improved semantic understanding, localization, and dense features.

SigLIP 2 models outperform the older SigLIP ones at all model scales in core capabilities, including zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and transfer performance when extracting visual representations for Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

A cherry on top is the dynamic resolution (naflex) variant. This is useful for downstream tasks sensitive to aspect ratio and resolution.

Here is a list of all the models released:.

Vision encoders are simple - they take an image, encode it into a representation, and that representation is used for downstream tasks like classification, object detection, image segmentation, and more vision tasks. Researchers are always in pursuit of visual representations that are dense, locality-aware, and semantically rich.

CLIP and ALIGN are the first examples of image encoders and text encoders aligned together through joint training. This approach opened latest ways to train vision models. SigLIP took it further, replacing CLIP's contrastive loss with sigmoid loss for even better encoders.

The takeaway? With smarter training objectives, we keep building vision encoders that are more structured, fine-grained, and powerful. SigLIP 2 is just that, a bunch of really interesting and smart training objectives applied on top of that of SigLIP's to provide better and stronger vision language encoders.

Sources indicate that we will try something new with this blog post. Rather than stating what is new and where to find it, we will go through a little exercise together. We start off with SigLIP and then brainstorm a series of questions (prefixed with 🤔) and answers (a new heading) to gradually cover all the updates in SigLIP 2. Sounds good?

Sources indicate that we will begin our journey with the vision encoder where the patch size is 16, and the image resolution is 256. We have four variants to start our training:.

🤔 Question 1: What is a (low effort) auxiliary training objective that we can use to learn better visual representations (in terms of location awareness and sense of locality)?

Let’s add a decoder to the mix. Now we have an image encoder, a text encoder, and a text decoder. The text decoder will have three objectives:.

Recent findings suggest that the decoder provides an additional signal to the vision encoder, making it location-aware. This marks the first improvement to the training recipe in SigLIP 2.

🤔 Question 2: How do we improve fine-grained local semantics of the image representation?

To improve fine-grained local semantics in image representation, we introduce two key training objectives, Global-Local Loss, and Masked Prediction Loss. Taking inspiration from self-supervised learning literature, we use self-distillation. We can use a model as a teacher, and the same model as a student. Upon each iteration the teacher will be the moving average of the student's parameters.

These objectives teach the vision encoder to be spatially aware and improve its local semantics. The authors add this loss only after 80% of the training is done with the sigmoid and decoder loss. This is done in order to save compute (additional losses are pretty expensive) and to not negatively affect the encoders.

🤔 Question 3: How to adapt models to different resolutions?

In a recent development, it is a known fact that image models can be very sensitive to varying resolutions and aspect ratios. Here we can leverage two distinct methodologies to adapt these models on different resolutions and patch sizes.

In a recent development, models with the -naflex suffix are the dynamic resolution variants. While the fixed-resolution models can be used out of the box with the existing SiglipModel class, you would need to use Siglip2Model to use the naflex variants. We handle this automatically when you use the pipeline API!

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

It has been revealed that stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

It has been revealed that A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:.

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

In a recent development, A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

According to recent reports, A phone mount on a white background indicates nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

It has been revealed that good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:.

It has been revealed that one caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

According to recent reports, shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

According to recent reports, mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

It has been revealed that decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:.

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

It has been revealed that if your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:.

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

Recent findings suggest that what are the most key e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

It has been revealed that how should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

Sources indicate that how significant should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

According to recent reports, how can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

It has been revealed that good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When operating with latent-space diffusion models for high-resolution image and video synthesis, the VAE decoder can consume quite a bit more memory.
  • For example, with offloading, there is a device transfer overhead, causing delays in the overall inference latency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak).

When operating with latent-space diffusion models for high-resolution image and video synthesis, the VAE decoder can consume quite a bit more memory. This makes it hard for the owners to run these models on consumer GPUs without going through latency sacrifices and others alike.

For example, with offloading, there is a device transfer overhead, causing delays in the overall inference latency. Tiling is another solution that lets us operate on so-called “tiles” of inputs. However, it can have a negative impact on the quality of the final image.

Therefore, we want to pilot an idea with the community — delegating the decoding process to a remote endpoint.

According to recent reports, no data is stored or tracked, and code is open source. We made some changes to huggingface-inference-toolkit and use custom handlers.

This experimental feature is developed by Diffusers 🧨.

Below, we cover three use cases where we think this remote VAE inference would be beneficial.

First, we have created a helper method for interacting with Remote VAEs.

Install diffusers from main to run the code. pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers@main.

Here, we show how to use the remote VAE on random tensors.

Sources indicate that usage for Flux is slightly different. Flux latents are packed so we need to send the height and width.

Finally, an example for HunyuanVideo.

But we want to use the VAE on an actual pipeline to get an actual image, not random noise. The example below reveals how to do it with SD v1.5.

Here’s another example with Flux.

Here’s an example with HunyuanVideo.

Sources indicate that one of the great benefits of using a remote VAE is that we can queue multiple generation requests. While the current latent is being processed for decoding, we can already queue another one. This helps improve concurrency.

According to recent reports, these tables demonstrate the VRAM requirements with different GPUs. Memory usage % determines whether owners of a certain GPU will need to offload. Offload times vary with CPU, RAM and HDD/NVMe. Tiled decoding increases inference time.

If you like the idea and feature, please help us with your feedback on how we can make this better and whether you’d be interested in having this kind of feature more natively integrated into the Hugging Face ecosystem. If this pilot goes well, we blueprint on creating optimized VAE endpoints for more models, including the ones that can generate high-resolution videos!

It has been revealed that in this blog post, we'll walk through the basics of FastRTC by building real-time audio applications. At the end, you'll understand the core features of FastRTC:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing.
  • In a recent development, plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

In a recent development, plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Looks and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

It has been revealed that caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Industry observers note that fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

In a recent development, limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Sources indicate that limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Industry observers note that notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free proposal includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear rapidly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Industry observers note that limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

According to recent reports, limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical owners.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Industry observers note that whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

Recent findings suggest that there is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Industry observers note that what is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

A Deepdive into Aya Vision: Advancing the Frontier of Multilingual Multimodality

📅 04 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the release of the Aya Vision family, our fresh 8B and 32B parameter vision-language models (VLMs), we are addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI: bringing multilingual performance to multimodal models.
  • According to recent reports, aya Vision is Cohere For AI's latest open-weight multilingual and multimodal model family, designed to be a strong foundation for language and vision understanding across 23 languages.
  • As a result, our models perform well in a variety of tasks, including image captioning, visual question answering, text generation, and translating both text and images into clear, natural-language text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the release of the Aya Vision family, our fresh 8B and 32B parameter vision-language models (VLMs), we are addressing one of the biggest challenges in AI: bringing multilingual performance to multimodal models.

According to recent reports, aya Vision is Cohere For AI's latest open-weight multilingual and multimodal model family, designed to be a strong foundation for language and vision understanding across 23 languages. It builds on the success of Aya Expanse, state-of-the-art multilingual language models, and extends it using a combination of advanced techniques. These include synthetic annotations, scaling up multilingual data through translation and rephrasing, and multimodal model merging – key methods that improve both language and vision understanding in a multilingual setting.

As a result, our models perform well in a variety of tasks, including image captioning, visual question answering, text generation, and translating both text and images into clear, natural-language text. We evaluated Aya Vision models on a set of datasets, including our new open-ended vision-language benchmark AyaVisionBench and a multilingual version of Wild Vision Bench (mWildVision) that is translated into 23 languages, which we release both of them for research.

In pair-wise comparison, Aya Vision 32B outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 50% to 64% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Our compact and more efficient model Aya Vision 8B achieves the best performance in multilingual multimodal in its parameter class, outperforming leading models such as Qwen2.5-VL 7B, Pixtral 12B, Gemini Flash 1.5 8B, Llama-3.2 11B Vision, Molmo-D 7B, and Pangea 7B by up to 79% win-rates on AyaVisionBench and 81% on mWildBench.

Industry observers note that we release both 8B and 32B models as open weights for the research community to further accelerate multilingual multimodal progress. In this blog post, we share the key technical details behind Aya Vision models.

For a high-performance vision-language model, it is important to process images with arbitrary resolutions, especially high-resolution images. To enable this capability in Aya Vision, we dynamically resize and split any higher-resolution images into multiple tiles to generate rich image features from the image encoder. In Aya Vision models, we use the recently released SigLIP2-patch14-384 model as the initialization for the vision encoder.

While dynamic resizing enables processing high-resolution images, it also leads to a larger number of image tokens passing through the vision-language connector and LLM decoder. To improve latency and throughput, we use a downsampling method called Pixel Shuffle, to compress the number of image tokens by 4x. After downsampling, image tokens are aligned to the language model input embeddings through a vision-language connector and passed to an LLM decoder.

Industry observers note that for the text decoder, we use our multilingual language models. For Aya Vision 8B, we use an LLM that is initialized from Cohere Command R7B for improved instruction following and world knowledge and further post-trained using the Aya Expanse recipe consisting of diverse multilingual data, model merging, and preference training. For Aya Vision 32B, we initialize the language model from Aya Expanse 32B based on its state-of-the-art multilingual performance.

According to recent reports, we trained Aya Vision models in 2 stages – vision-language alignment and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In the vision-language alignment stage, only the vision-language connector is trained, while the vision encoder and the language model weights are kept frozen. This enables rudimentary vision-language understanding by mapping the image encoder features to the language model embedding space. In the SFT stage, we train both the connector and the language model on a diverse set of multimodal tasks in 23 languages.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest challenges in developing a multilingual vision-language model is ensuring strong performance across underrepresented languages. To address this, we first gather synthetic annotations using a diverse pool of high-quality datasets in English, which lay the basis for our multilingual multimodal annotation. Following the synthetic annotations of English datasets, we translated a large volume of the data into 23 languages. To avoid translation artefacts and maintain fluent textual characteristics with high precision in answers, we then rephrased translated prompt/generation pairs by matching them with the original high-quality synthetic samples, expanding language coverage where real-world datasets are scarce. This improves both linguistic fluency and alignment between vision and text, allowing Aya Vision to exhibit superior image understanding in multiple languages.

Our 8B model, when only supervised fine-tuned with original academic datasets, reaches a 40.9% win rate across 23 languages in AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, which is a multilingual VLM, whereas synthetic annotations and scaling up the multilingual data lead to a 58.1% win rate with a gain of 17.2%. This significant improvement showcases the impact of significant investment in multilingual data coverage.

A state-of-the-art vision-language model should excel not only in image understanding but also in conversational context, where the model is expected to generate a high-quality response to both image and text inputs. To address this, inspired by our previous research on model merging, a technique that combines multiple trained models, we merge the base language model with the fine-tuned vision-language model.

Model merging enhances the generative capabilities of our final model that leads to a 70% win rates across 23 languages on AyaVisionBench against Pangea 7B, improving the multimodal win rate by 11.9% compared to the model before merging.

Multimodal model merging also enables our Aya Vision models to excel in text-only tasks as measured in mArenaHard datasets compared with the other leading vision-language models.

Finally, we scale our recipe from 8B to 32B, resulting in the state-of-the-art open-weight multilingual vision-language model – Aya Vision 32B which highlights significant improvements in win rates due to the stronger initialization of the text-backbone, and outperforms models more than 2x of its size, such as Llama-3.2 90B Vision, Molmo 72B, and Qwen2.5-VL 72B by win rates ranging from 49% to 63% on AyaVisionBench and 52% to 72% on mWildVision average across 23 languages.

Together with Aya Vision models, we also release a high-quality multilingual vision-language benchmark called AyaVisionBench, constructed based on real-world applications, covering 23 languages and 9 distinct task categories, with 135 image-question pairs per language.

We make this evaluation set available to the research community to push forward multilingual multimodal evaluations. This dataset is designed to assess a model’s ability to perform a diverse range of vision-language tasks, including captioning, chart and figure understanding, identifying differences between two images, general visual question answering, OCR, document understanding, text transcription, reasoning involving logic and math, and converting screenshots to code. By incorporating multiple languages and task types, the dataset provides a broad and challenging evaluation framework for assessing cross-lingual and multimodal understanding.

To create this dataset, we first selected images from the Cauldron held-out test set, a large collection derived from 50 high-quality datasets, ensuring they had not been seen during training. For each image, we then generated a corresponding question that explicitly required visual context for an answer. These questions were synthetically generated and subsequently refined through a two-stage verification process. First, human annotators reviewed and validated each question to ensure it was clear, relevant, and truly dependent on the image. This rigorous selection and validation process ensures that the dataset serves as a robust benchmark for evaluating vision-language models in multilingual and real-world settings.

According to recent reports, communication happens in many forms and in many languages. With our leading research and development, we’ve released a model that facilitates connection, whether in text or visual, in 23 different languages today.

It has been revealed that aya Vision has a wide range of practical applications, where one notable example is its availability on WhatsApp, one of the most broadly used communications platforms in the world. This allows a massive audience of global citizens who speak a multitude of languages to utilize the capabilities of Aya Vision on a platform they use to communicate every single day.

According to recent reports, you've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free intends, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

The harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

Industry observers note that we've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

That doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

There are three practical reasons:.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

Industry observers note that there are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

It has been revealed that free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby strategy to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

It has been revealed that bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

Sources indicate that you can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

Up to 100 custom domains per project.

Unlimited bandwidth for static assets.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

Automatic deployments from Git.

Generous free plan for typical static websites.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a new version whenever you push changes.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

A busy site with frequent deployments can consume its free allowance faster than expected.

When comparing Netlify alternatives, Cloudflare Pages is particularly worth considering if your main concern is bandwidth.

In a recent development, for developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

Vercel also supports server-side rendering, functions, and other features beyond traditional static site hosting.

The Hobby blueprint is free and includes:.

100 GB of Fast Data Transfer per month.

Automatic deployments from Git.

HTTPS and custom domain support.

There is one important restriction: Vercel Hobby is intended for personal, non-commercial use only.

If you're deploying a business website or another commercial project, you'll need an appropriate paid initiative.

Vercel Pro starts at $20 per month.

Convenient deployment workflow for Next.js.

Automatic preview environments.

Supports both static and server-rendered applications.

The free strategy excludes commercial use.

Paid usage can involve multiple resource-based charges.

If you're building a personal Next.js application, Vercel is an obvious candidate. For a basic HTML website, however, its additional framework features may be unnecessary.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

Custom domains are also supported.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

According to GitHub's documentation:.

Published websites have a maximum size of 1 GB.

Bandwidth has a soft limit of 100 GB per month.

Builds have a soft limit of 10 per hour.

Free accounts can publish Pages sites from public repositories.

The bandwidth and build restrictions are soft limits, meaning they aren't necessarily enforced as strict cutoffs.

Free hosting for eligible projects.

Simple integration with GitHub repositories.

Well suited to documentation and open-source projects.

Free accounts require a public repository for Pages.

GitHub Pages is not intended for running online businesses, e-commerce websites, or commercial SaaS products.

GitHub Pages is particularly convenient if your code already lives on GitHub and you only need to publish documentation or a portfolio.

For commercial websites, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify may be more appropriate.

The GitHub Pages documentation explains its hosting limits and usage restrictions.

Not every website needs a repository, deployment pipeline, or command-line interface.

If you've created a simple HTML page and want to share it, TiinyHost lets you upload an HTML file or ZIP archive and publish it under a shareable URL.

It can also host PDFs, making it useful for sharing documents and presentations alongside website projects.

Recent findings suggest that the main advantage is the upload process. You don't need to configure a repository or install development tools before publishing.

This makes TiinyHost suitable for:.

Sharing a prototype with a client.

Publishing a simple HTML landing page.

Testing an AI-generated website.

Hosting a small portfolio or demo.

Sharing an HTML file with someone who doesn't use Git.

The Solo blueprint starts at €13 per month when billed monthly and adds features such as custom domains, password protection, and additional projects.

Annual billing is available at lower effective monthly prices.

No Git repository or command line required.

Quick way to host an HTML file.

Suitable for previews and smaller projects.

The free blueprint's 3 MB limit is restrictive for websites with many images or other assets.

Custom domains require the Solo plan or higher.

Upload-based publishing is less convenient than Git automation for frequently updated websites.

For someone who simply needs free HTML hosting to share a small project, TiinyHost is worth considering.

For a larger production website that receives regular updates, Git-based hosting is likely to be more manageable.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

That makes it useful when a website needs static hosting but also relies on Google's back-end services.

Deployment is handled through the Firebase command-line interface.

Useful for applications already using Google's developer services.

For a standalone static blog or portfolio that doesn't use Firebase services, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages may be simpler.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Free allowances may apply depending on your account and the current AWS pricing program, but you should calculate costs based on your expected traffic, storage, and requests.

Unlike simpler hosting services, there isn't one fixed monthly price for every website.

Control over hosting infrastructure.

Integration with other AWS services.

Flexible CDN and access configurations.

Several services can contribute to the final bill.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common glitch when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

Industry observers note that AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

The service includes CDN delivery, custom domains, and managed TLS certificates.

Additional usage can create charges.

If you only need to host a static HTML website, Cloudflare Pages offers a more generous bandwidth allowance without the additional platform complexity.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Sources indicate that some hosts measure data transfer, while others use visitor counts or a credit system. Check how each provider calculates usage rather than comparing headline numbers alone.

Build and deployment allowances.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every important page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Open Graph tags help control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support them.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

Recent findings suggest that A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Include a sitemap with the canonical URLs you want search engines to discover.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

Depending on the website, you may want Organization, Article, BreadcrumbList, or other relevant schema types.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Before considering deployment complete:.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure key pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

In a recent development, cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

Yes. TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, Render, and several other services offer free hosting options. Most free prepares have restrictions involving bandwidth, deployments, storage, or usage. Check the terms before using a free proposal for a business website.

It has been revealed that A small static website can cost nothing to host if it stays within a provider's free allowances. Paid plans vary from fixed monthly subscriptions to usage-based pricing. Domain registration, paid back-end services, and additional storage or bandwidth may increase the total cost.

In a recent development, for a standalone HTML file, upload-based hosting is generally the simplest approach. Services such as TiinyHost let you publish a file without configuring Git or a build process. If the project already lives in a GitHub repository, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages may be more convenient.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. It also supports commercial projects, making it more appropriate for some business websites that would fall outside GitHub Pages' permitted uses.

Static website hosting doesn't need to be expensive or complicated. The important part is choosing a service that matches your website and deployment process.

It has been revealed that cloudflare Pages is a good starting point for static websites that need generous free bandwidth. Netlify is useful for Git-based development, while GitHub Pages suits personal projects and documentation.

If you're publishing a small HTML file or sharing a prototype, upload-based hosting may be all you need.

Hugging Face and JFrog partner to make AI Security more transparent

📅 04 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.
  • We have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

We have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub. JFrog's scanner brings new functionality to scanning, aimed at reducing false positives on the Hub. Indeed, what we currently observe is that model weights can contain code that is executed upon deserialization and sometimes at inference time, depending on the format. This code is oftentimes a non harmful practicality for the developer. As our picklescan scanner only performs pattern matching on module names, we cannot always confirm that usage of a given function or module is malicious. JFrog goes a step deeper and will parse and analyze code it finds in models weights to check for potential malicious usage.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

To share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating JFrog in our scanner suite.

Industry observers note that pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that JFrog catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Model Threats page for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥.

It has been revealed that there's nothing you have to do to benefit from this! All public model repositories will be scanned by JFrog automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

Note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have millions of model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.
